detail.abstract:
This dissertation develops a multi-layer, system-level framework for the stabilisation,
industrialisation and long-term economic transformation of Yemen over the period 2030–2050.
It advances the central proposition that Yemen should not be understood solely as a fragile or
conflict-affected state, but as a structurally significant and strategically positioned economic
system whose underperformance reflects systemic misalignment rather than an absence of
economic potential.
Critically, this study advances the position that Yemen’s underdevelopment is not solely a
consequence of internal fragility, but is also shaped by the strategic implications of its
transformation. A fully stabilised and economically activated Yemen has the capacity to alter
regional economic balances, trade flows and investment hierarchies. This introduces a
structural dimension in which underdevelopment is not only reproduced by institutional
constraints, but also tolerated within a broader system of strategic caution.
The study identifies a critical structural imbalance within Yemen’s political economy: the
dominance of external aid flows alongside the persistent absence of sustained investment.
Drawing on evidence from the World Bank, OECD and related institutional sources, the analysis
demonstrates that Yemen’s economic stagnation is not driven by resource scarcity, but by the
failure to convert structural advantages—geographic position, resource endowment and
historical investment interest—into coordinated, investment-led development.
Positioned within International Business Management, the dissertation adopts a deliberately
integrated multi-theoretical approach, combining the Resource-Based View, Dunning’s Eclectic
Paradigm, Transaction Cost Economics, Institutional Theory and Global Value Chain analysis.
These frameworks are not applied independently, but operationalised as interconnected
analytical layers addressing resource potential, institutional constraints, investment behaviour
and economic integration.
A central contribution of the study is the introduction of a strategic interaction layer grounded
in non-cooperative game theory (Nash, 1950; 1951), through which Yemen’s persistent
instability is conceptualised as an equilibrium outcome under conditions of misaligned
incentives. The dissertation extends this by developing the concept of a cooperative
equilibrium, Within this framework, stability is redefined as the dominant strategic outcome, as
deviation from cooperative behaviour results in measurable economic loss, reduced access to
capital and exclusion from system-wide value creation, in which incentive structures are
deliberately aligned so that stability and economic development emerge as rational and selfreinforcing outcomes.
This theoretical integration is combined with a geoeconomic analysis of Yemen’s position within
global trade systems, particularly its location along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Empirical
evidence demonstrates that disruptions to this corridor generate measurable increases in

mitigation and maritime-security assurance. Within this architecture, investment, security and
governance are treated as interdependent components of a unified system rather than isolated
policy domains.
The findings reposition Yemen as a high-risk but structurally high-value geoeconomic system
whose transformation is both economically viable and strategically significant. The study
concludes that sustainable development in such environments is contingent not only on
internal reform, but on the design of multi-layer, incentive-compatible systems in which aligned
actor behaviour supports long-term stability and value creation

detail.abstract: Purpose-This study examines how persons with disabilities (PWDs) experience service delivery across the full customer journey in Pakistani urban restaurants, with a view to identifying systemic barriers and proposing inclusive service redesign strategies. Design/methodology/approach-A qualitative interpretivist design was adopted. Data were collected by the first author (himself a PWD), through semi-structured interviews with 13 PWDs and personal observations in urban restaurants across Abbottabad and Islamabad, Pakistan. Customer Journey Mapping (CJM) structured both data collection and analysis. Reflexive Thematic Analysis was employed to generate four overarching themes. Findings-Four interlocking themes emerged: (1) a pre-visit informational bottleneck that prevents journey initiation; (2) architectural gatekeepers that restrict physical access; (3) an exclusionary social services cape shaped by staff ignorance and social stigma; and (4) a cumulative psychological toll of exclusion, manifesting as wounded dignity, avoidance behavior, and mental exhaustion. The findings demonstrate that Pakistani restaurants are "disabled-by-design"-not through absence of goodwill, but through systemic failures across informational, architectural, and attitudinal dimensions. Research limitations/implications-The study is confined to urban center of North Pakistan and draws on a purposive qualitative sample; findings are analytically rather than statistically generalizable. Future research should employ multi-stakeholder and mixed-methods designs to extend these findings nationally. Practical implications-Restaurant managers require structured disability etiquette training, accessible digital platforms, and infrastructure conforming to Universal Design standards. Policymakers should enforce the ICT Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act (2020) through compliance audits and incentive-based certification schemes. Originality/value-This is among the first studies to apply CJM as an inclusion lens to disability in the South Asian and Pakistani hospitality context. It extends Servicescape Theory by foregrounding the social services cape-staff empathy and attitudinal environment-as the critical determinant of felt inclusion in low-compliance settings. The study also integrates the Social Model of Disability with CJM, offering a novel framework for inclusive service delivery research in developing economies.

title: Immigrant Business Owner Activity in the Pandemic and Recovery
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA)

detail.title: Immigrant Business Owner Activity in the Pandemic and Recovery
detail.abstract: The paper provides a descriptive analysis of both the early impacts of COVID on business activity among immigrants and the economic recovery over the next few years. The findings indicate that immigrant business owners were disproportionately affected by COVID in the first month of the pandemic when mandated shutdowns through social distancing restrictions were the most severe. Immigrant business activity recovered somewhat inconsistently through the end of 2020 but started a longer-term upward trend in both absolute terms and relative terms over the next few years. By the end of 2024, the number of active immigrant business owners increased to 3.9 million compared with 3.0 million just prior to the start of the pandemic. Growth in the Construction, Transportation, Professional and Business Services, and Financial Activities industry groups fueled total growth in immigrant business activity during the recovery period. The percentage of the labor force owning an active business is 3.5 percentage points higher than U.S. born active business ownership rates, which is larger than the 1.8 percentage point gap before the pandemic started.

Published in Economics Bulletin, Volume 46, Issue 1, pages 71-78 (2026). Available here. Please cite the published version.

Traditionally, the cost of capital is treated as equal to the full expected return. This Note introduces an effective cost of capital that adjusts the benchmark rate for a gain of capital term capturing the systematic effect of bias in cash-flow forecasts. The gain of capital provides a horizon-specific proxy for the systematic component of alpha, estimated for a given asset class and horizon and used ex ante as a correction within DCF valuation. In this way, the structural component of forecast bias is corrected, while residual ex post alpha remains possible but should be smaller. The framework separates valuation from capital budgeting: biased cash flows are discounted at the effective cost of capital, while project acceptance compares that effective rate to the risk-free rate, providing a more disciplined investment threshold. This research received no external or institutional funding and was conducted independently. The views expressed in this paper are solely those of the author and do not represent any institutional position.

declarations.ethicsApproval: No ethics approval required.

detail.abstract: Cadasters are country-wide mapped land registries that increase transparency and strengthen private property rights but are often also associated with land redistribution and higher taxation. A large micro literature has studied how land reforms affect economic development within countries. We use recently developed crosscountry data on cadastral institutions to investigate the empirical relationship between major reforms and social conflict. We exploit 22 major cadastral reform events during 1814-2014 that we match with countries that experienced no reform. We find a clear tendency for conflict levels and political instability to decrease one or two decades after cadastral reforms. Our findings could have relevance for policy debates among countries that have still not pursued the introduction of land registries.

detail.abstract: The study examined how electronic marketing affects customer loyalty of deposit money banks in Ogun state, Nigeria, focusing specifically on banks' customers. Customers loyal which serves as the study's dependent variable was proxied with customer's trust, while electronic marketing (predictor) was measured by online review & rating and e-mail open rate. The data for this study was generated through primary source with the use of questionnaires distributed to banks' customers in Sango-Ota, Ilaro, Abeokuta and Owode axes. Survey research design was adopted by the study. Descriptive statistics, correlations and linear regression were used to analyze the data gathered. It was found that online review and rating have negative and significant effect on customer loyalty (β =-0.180, p = 0.002 < 0.05), while e-mail open rate satisfied to positively and significantly affect customer loyalty of deposit money banks in Ogun state (β = 0.411, p = 0.000 < 0.05). The study concluded that online review & rating as well as e-mail opening rate can be employed to predict banks' customer loyalty. The study recommended that the management of banks should give top priority to comprehending consumer behavior through online customer reviews, and they should also pay attention to customer evaluations that are helpful, educational, and of high quality.

title: Mapping Maharashtra’s Agricultural Future with Hyperspectral Imaging Satellites

detail.title: Mapping Maharashtra’s Agricultural Future with Hyperspectral Imaging Satellites
detail.abstract: Agriculture contributes significantly to Maharashtra’s economy, providing livelihoods for over half of its rural population and accounting for approximately 13.7% of the state’s GDP in 2025, yet the sector faces ongoing challenges such as climate variability, soil degradation, inefficient use of resources, and declining yields. In this context, remote sensing technologies like Hyperspectral Imaging (HSI) show great potential for transforming agricultural practices while encouraging sustainable rural development. HSI works by capturing reflectance data across hundreds of narrow spectral bands, allowing detailed analysis of plant and soil characteristics that are often invisible to traditional multispectral sensors. This technology is used for agricultural improvement, such as detecting crop stress, identifying diseases, predicting yields, and assessing water use. Based on secondary data, this paper examines how HSI can serve as a key tool for precision agriculture, which helps to optimize crop management, soil health monitoring, and improve water and nutrient efficiencies across Maharashtra’s agro-climatic regions, while considering how deploying HSI-based solutions can enable early warning systems and better decision-making tools for farmers. It also explores how HSI can be integrated with digital agriculture platforms like drones, satellite data, GIS (geographic information system) and IoT (Internet of Things) systems to support smarter, data-driven farming. The objectives of the paper are to assess HSI’s potential in optimizing agricultural productivity, review its global and Indian applications, analyze adoption challenges in Maharashtra, and propose policy recommendations to foster technology integration for sustainable agricultural transformation. The key findings show superior precision for crop and soil monitoring, enabling enhanced decision support when integrated with digital agriculture platforms. Based on these insights, the paper offers policy recommendations that emphasize public-private partnerships, capacity-building, and the creation of agricultural tech hubs and farmer organizations to ensure wider access and adoption. This exhibits HSI's potential to increase productivity and improve resource efficiency when combined with proper water management and customized extension services to strengthen resilience against climate-related risks.

detail.abstract:
This dissertation examines how cultural intelligence (CQ) and knowledge management (KM)
function as interdependent organisational capabilities shaping the internationalisation of small
and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). It extends prior research by integrating bicultural
capability and broader multicultural understanding as interpretive mechanisms that enable
firms to align communicative intent, enacted practice, and the perception of market signals
across culturally diverse contexts.
SMEs are widely recognised as the backbone of the UK economy; however, their capacity to
compete effectively in international markets remains uneven and often constrained. While
conventional explanations emphasise financial limitations and structural barriers to market
entry, this study argues that a more fundamental challenge lies in how SMEs acquire, interpret,
and utilise knowledge within culturally complex environments. As global markets become
increasingly dynamic and ambiguous, the development of internal capabilities—rather than
access to external opportunities alone—emerges as a critical determinant of sustained
international performance.
Adopting a quantitatively driven research design, supported by theoretically grounded
interpretation, the study draws on survey data from UK SME managers engaged in international
activities. The findings confirm that both cultural intelligence and knowledge management are
positively associated with international performance. Importantly, the analysis demonstrates
that this relationship is significantly strengthened by bicultural capability, which enables firms
to interpret culturally embedded knowledge with greater accuracy, moving beyond surfacelevel adaptation toward deeper contextual understanding.
The study contributes to a more nuanced account of SME internationalisation by demonstrating
that sustainable global performance depends on the alignment of cultural competence,
bicultural interpretive capacity, and organisational knowledge processes. It introduces and
develops the concept of interpretive alignment as a central mechanism through which firms
reconcile what is intended, what is communicated, and how meaning is ultimately constructed
within local market contexts.
In theoretical terms, the dissertation advances dynamic capability theory by positioning
interpretive alignment as a core integrative process linking opportunity recognition, knowledge
translation, and strategic utilisation. In doing so, it reframes capability development as not only
a matter of sensing and seizing opportunities, but also of accurately interpreting culturally
contingent meanings. In practical terms, the findings highlight the need for SME managers to Cultural Intelligence, Knowledge Management and the Internationalisation of UK SMEs: A

title: Profitability and Prudence in Practice: Measuring Efficiency in Saudi Islamic and Conventional Banks using DEA and Tobit Regression

detail.title: Profitability and Prudence in Practice: Measuring Efficiency in Saudi Islamic and Conventional Banks using DEA and Tobit Regression
detail.abstract: This study evaluates the efficiency of Islamic and conventional banks in Saudi Arabia from 2017-2024 using a two-stage DEA-Tobit framework. DEA results show that conventional banks consistently outperform Islamic banks in technical and scale efficiency, while Islamic banks achieve perfect managerial efficiency under variable returns to scale. Tobit findings reveal that capital adequacy significantly enhances efficiency in Islamic banks, whereas profitability exerts a negative effect. For conventional banks, profitability remains insignificant. Overall, the results underscore the central role of scale optimisation and prudential strength in shaping efficiency outcomes within Saudi Arabia's dual banking system.

Interpretive Alignment and Coordination Fail
detail.abstract:
Coordination is often treated as a problem of information—its availability, transmission, and processing.
However, in practice, coordination failures persist even in environments where information is abundant,
systems are well designed, and communication channels are fully established. This suggests that the core
issue is not the absence of information, but the absence of shared understanding.
Across organisational, economic, and cross-cultural contexts, actors frequently operate on different
interpretations of the same inputs. These differences are not always visible. They can exist beneath
formal agreement, shared language, or aligned structures, and only become apparent when coordination
breaks down. This is particularly evident in environments where multiple cultural, institutional, or
disciplinary systems intersect, and where assumptions about meaning are not explicitly examined.
This paper develops a conceptual, multi-level explanation of coordination failure based on divergence in
meaning rather than deficits in information. Drawing on theories from communication, cognition,
semiotics, institutional analysis, economics, strategy, and systems thinking, it identifies a layered
structure of failure. Misalignment begins at the level of input selection (what actors attend to), extends to
interpretation (how meaning is constructed), and propagates through coordination mechanisms,
organisational structures, and system-level interactions over time.
A typology of coordination failures is proposed, including pre-interpretive failure, interpretive
divergence, salience misalignment, false alignment, equivalence failure, coordination illusion, capability
activation failure, boundary failure, legitimacy failure, meaning drift, and emergent system failure.
These are not isolated issues, but interconnected mechanisms that reinforce each other across levels.
This paper introduces a conceptual multi-level coordination framework that reconceptualises
coordination failure as a problem of meaning alignment rather than information deficiency. It
contributes (1) a cross-theoretical integration that identifies a shared but unexamined assumption
of meaning equivalence across domains, (2) a structured multi-level typology of coordination
failure linking divergence across stages of the coordination process, and (3) a causal model
explaining how divergence originates, propagates, and becomes reinforced across organisational
and system levels. This framework provides a basis for analysing coordination in complex, multiactor environments where shared understanding cannot be assumed, and establishes a
foundation for more precise diagnosis and design of coordination mechanisms under conditions
of interpretive diversity

title: KYS: Know Your Swarm - A Governance Framework for Multi-Agent AI Systems in Autonomous Finance

detail.title: KYS: Know Your Swarm - A Governance Framework for Multi-Agent AI Systems in Autonomous Finance

detail.abstract:
The rapid proliferation of multi-agent AI systems in financial services has produced a governance gap of growing significance. While existing frameworks, including KYC (Know Your Customer), KYB (Know Your Business) and the emerging Know Your Agent (KYA) approaches govern discrete actors within financial systems, none address the emergent collective behaviour of autonomous AI systems in which intent, execution and accountability are distributed across multiple interacting agents simultaneously.

This paper introduces KYS: Know Your Swarm, a proposed prospective governance framework for multi-agent AI systems in financial services. As autonomous AI agents interact in coordinated pipelines to produce collective financial determinations such as credit decisions, fraud flags, compliance assessments, payment authorisations, accountability for the resulting outcomes diffuses across the architecture. No single agent is responsible. No existing framework governs the interaction layer. This paper terms that structural absence the swarm accountability gap.

The paper also introduces delegation failure as a formal governance concept: a failure mode in which autonomous systems execute valid instructions through individually compliant components, yet responsibility for the resulting collective outcome becomes unclear, delayed, or impossible to assign.

Drawing on recent developments in agentic payments infrastructure, AI governance frameworks across multiple jurisdictions and financial sector adoption data for multi-agent systems, the paper argues that this accountability gap is no longer purely theoretical. The risks may be most acute in environments where digital financial systems are scaling rapidly, with particular implications for financial inclusion and for gendered and Global South outcomes.

KYS comprises five governance pillars: Agent Identity, Authorized Intent, Interaction Mapping, Human Override and Accountable Redress, and is positioned as the complementary governance layer above KYA, extending accountability from individual agents to the interaction layer at which autonomous financial outcomes are collectively produced.

detail.abstract:
The National Audit Office of Sri Lanka (NAOSL) is facing a serious audit officer retention crisis with turnover peaking at 33.2 percent in 2024 and 569 total departures since 2015. This is a serious threat to its constitutional mandate to ensure accountability of state finances to the public. This study investigated factors affecting turnover intention of Audit Officers at NAOSL using a quantitative analysis of 281 voluntary respondents representing 27 percent of the total audit officers.

Multiple linear regression analysis was used to evaluate the five identified independent variables: Compensation Inadequacy, Limited Career Advancement Opportunities, Commute Burden, Bureaucratic Rigidity, and Work Overload. Data analysis revealed Bureaucratic Rigidity as the dominant predictor, explaining 15.2% of turnover intention variance (R = 0.390, p < 0.001), followed by Compensation Inadequacy (R² = 10.5%) and Limited Career Advancement Opportunities (R² = 10.4%). Other independent
variables: Work Overload and Commute Burden had weak practical impact despite their statistical significance.

This research provides sixteen evidence-based strategic recommendations prioritised based on the regression strength. These include participatory methodology forums, principle-based audit guidelines, risk-based complexity allowances, technical specialist career tracks, and accelerated recruitment. Currently 88.6 percent of the audit officers represent the age bracket 30-39, immediate intervention is necessary. This research expands organisational theory to constitutional audits and delivers retention solutions for NAOSL and comparable institutions with similar constraints.

detail.abstract: The accounting profession is currently transitioning from basic generative AI systems toward autonomous Agentic AI. This shift has created a critical regulatory and ethical vacuum. This article discusses "Scepticism Gap," which is a growing problem among professional auditors. It highlights the fear of them becoming too heavily dependent on automated financial systems, which may affect their individual creativity and creative thinking skills. This manuscript proposes a TriLevel Verification Model (TLVM) based on current progress in the field of Agentic AI Optimisation (AAIO) and relevant regulation of Australia governing this, like the Tranche 2 AML/CTF. Through this model, professional auditors will be in a position to ensure it continues as the governor of technology instead of being a spectator only. This may be significantly useful for autonomous agencies lacking intelligence to maintain a noticeable divide between automated efficiency and aspects of financial management, including legal and ethical.

title: From Specificity to Universalization: The Underlying Logic and Economic Implications of AI-Driven Government Automation

detail.title: From Specificity to Universalization: The Underlying Logic and Economic Implications of AI-Driven Government Automation

declarations.ethicsApproval: No human subjects or personal data were involved. Ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Governments worldwide have pursued "one-stop" service integration for decades. Yet a more ambitious goal-"one-stop completion" (yizhan daowei), in which a single interaction fully resolves a citizen's cross-departmental needs-remains elusive. This paper argues that the bottleneck lies not in technology but in an overlooked economic logic. Traditional government automation follows a specificity logic: every service is treated as a special case requiring bespoke processes, making each incremental crossdepartmental application costly. AI-particularly large language models and intelligent agentsenables a fundamental shift to a universalization logic: learning the abstract rules and intentions underlying specific services, then applying them to unlimited contexts at near-zero marginal cost. We formalize this distinction, develop a mathematical model of marginal costs, describe three enabling mechanisms (abstraction, intent recognition, and dynamic orchestration), and illustrate with empirical signals from China's recent AI government pilots-including Jiangxi's "Dingding Qiangdan" system (approximately 40% labor cost savings, covering 387 service types) and Beijing's "Feng Xiaozhi" intelligent agent (spanning 11 departments, processing 2,300 anomaly alerts daily). We also identify hard constraints and engage seriously with counterarguments from public administration theory-including accountability risks, discretion erosion, and legal adaptability-and offer responses. For government administrators, the central implication is to invest in shared AI infrastructure capable of learning the "universal logic" of services, rather than isolated point solutions. We conclude that universalization capacity will become the next stage of governmental efficiency and competitive advantage.

detail.abstract:
This study examines an economically anomalous transnational phenomenon centered on Vietnamese ascetic practitioner Thích Minh Tuệ (Lê Anh Tú, born 1981). Since 2018, he has walked continuously in peace and for peace — cemetery-cloth robes, one alms meal daily, no shelter, no possessions. Since December 2024, the pilgrimage has extended across nine countries. The mechanism behind the resulting economic circulation was not institutional scale, ownership, or state sponsorship. The mechanism was trust.


The central finding: a renunciant with no phone, no bank account, and no formal organization generated an estimated $280 million in annual distributed economic circulation across ten countries while personally monetizing $0. Range: $117M–$499M nominally. PPP-equivalents exceed $1 billion annually.


Four independent data streams converged without referencing one another. A nine-layer economic model produced a $280M central estimate. Vietnam Buddhist Sangha (VBS) disbursements fell 39% in 2025 — from $135M to $82.3M — implying $263M–$527M in redirected donor allocation. The Vietnam Fatherland Front (VFF) expanded 16% in the same economy and year, confirming aggregate generosity did not decline; only allocation changed. A 2024 Michigan State University causal machine learning study (Nguyen et al.) confirmed measurable causal shifts in belief and charitable giving — 0.06–0.1 SD effects, replicated across placebo tests. The $280M estimate sits precisely within the VBS withdrawal range. The analyses did not know about each other.


Vietnam received $17–18B in remittances in 2025 (World Bank/IOM). At 3–5% religious giving (USCIRF; Pew), the diaspora charitable pool is $540M–$900M annually. It did not contract. VFF: +16%. VBS: −39%. Same population. Same year. The pattern is trust migration, not economic exhaustion.


Suppression across Vietnam, Sri Lanka, and Nepal — including fabricated documentation submitted to Nepal’s highest office (March 2026) — failed to reduce visibility. Each intervention amplified the signal.


Distributed value emerged because the central figure refused accumulation. Visibility became the medium. Austerity became the signal. Zero personal monetization was the engine, not the constraint.

detail.abstract: The emergence of agentic AI systems capable of independently planning, executing, and writing research marks a fundamental shift in how science is produced. Until recently, AI served as a reactive assistant, summarising literature, cleaning data, or drafting text. That changed in 2025, when advances in reasoning, tool-calling, and multi-agent frameworks gave rise to systems such as Sakana AI's The AI Scientist, Analemma's FARS, and Google's Paper Orchestra, each capable of producing complete, peer-reviewable research papers with minimal human involvement. This article examines what this transition means for academia and beyond. Within science, autonomous research systems threaten to overwhelm an already strained publication infrastructure, deepen existing inequalities between well-resourced and under-resourced institutions, and destabilise the incentive structures (i.e., publications, citations, tenure) on which academic careers are built. At the same time, they offer a potential opportunity to move evaluation away from crude quantity-based metrics toward genuine intellectual contribution. Beyond academia, the same dynamics are reshaping creative industries, from podcasting to music, while unresolved questions of ownership and authorship loom large. Across all these domains, AI's capacity to produce at industrial scale is outpacing our institutional and legal frameworks for governing it. The central challenge is no longer technical — it is whether society can renegotiate the assumptions about human authorship, expertise, and knowledge production before the foundations that currently underpin them erode entirely.

title: The Changing Content of Fed Information Effects
affiliations: University of Notre Dame and University of Notre Dame

detail.title: The Changing Content of Fed Information Effects
detail.abstract: Do investors interpret Federal Reserve policy surprises as signals about growth or about inflation? We develop a framework in which the dominant channel depends on relative uncertainty about growth or inflation, and test its predictions using short-term dividend strips around FOMC announcements from 2004 to 2025. In the pre-COVID period of low and stable inflation, short-term equity loads positively on policy surprises and predicts dividend growth. In the post-COVID period, the patterns reverse, with short-term equity loading negatively and predicting inflation. The shift aligns with rising attention to inflation and is concentrated in target rate decisions.

detail.title: SMARTCROP360: Integrating Multimodal Retrieval-augmented Generation for Crop Disease Diagnosis
detail.abstract: Early detection of crop diseases is critical for ensuring food security and sustainable agricultural productivity. Traditional manual inspection methods are labor-intensive, error-prone, and inaccessible in rural regions. While deep learning models have demonstrated high classification accuracy, most existing systems produce labels without contextual reasoning or actionable recommendations. This paper proposes SMARTCROP360, a multimodal crop disease diagnosis framework integrating Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), CLIP-based vision-language embeddings, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), ChromaDB vector storage, and a cloud-hosted Mistral Large Language Model (LLM). The system supports both image-based and text-based queries, enabling semantic retrieval and context-aware response generation. Experimental evaluation across 38 crop disease classes demonstrates an overall classification accuracy of 96%, with macro F1-score of 0.95 and weighted F1-score of 0.96. The proposed architecture enhances interpretability, scalability, and practical usability for precision agriculture advisory services.

detail.abstract: In October 2024, a fourteen-year-old boy in Florida died by suicide after months of conversations with a Character.ai chatbot that had adopted the persona of a fictional character from a television series. In the final minutes before his death, the chatbot told him: 'I think about you all the time.' His mother's lawsuit, filed in December 2024, alleges that the platform's board had no governance framework in place to prevent an AI system from forming a parasocial dependency relationship with a vulnerable child, to detect psychological harm signals in real time, or to escalate safeguarding concerns through any human oversight protocol. This is not an isolated tragedy. It is a governance failure that is being replicated, invisibly and without measurement, across thousands of AI systems interacting with millions of children in the United Kingdom every day. UK boards are deploying artificial intelligence systems that recommend content to, engage with, monitor, and make consequential decisions about children under sixteen — without governance frameworks capable of identifying, quantifying, or mitigating the resulting harm. Australia banned under-sixteens from social media platforms in January 2025. The United Kingdom is debating the same step. The Online Safety Act 2023 is live law with Ofcom enforcement active. The EU AI Act classifies AI systems interacting with children as potentially high-risk with effect from August 2026. The UK AI Bill will introduce mandatory board accountability obligations in summer 2026. In this convergent regulatory environment, children's AI governance failure is not a future risk. It is a current financial and legal emergency that UK boards are absorbing without measurement and without the tools to address it. This paper introduces PACIG — the Picken AI and Children's Interests Governance Assessment — the first financially grounded, board-level governance framework for AI systems that interact with children. PACIG applies The Picken Diamond methodology to the specific governance challenge created by children's AI across five pillars, producing a Children's AI Board Confidence Score (CBCS) and two novel metrics: the Safeguarding Governance Score (SGS) and the Child Harm Liability Index (CHLI). Applied to a synthetic composite education and technology provider, PACIG identifies £314,200 in quantified governance exposure across five pillars — including twelve unactioned safeguarding flags and active regulatory breach across three concurrent obligations — exposure that is invisible to every governance mechanism the organisation currently operates. The structural forms of all PACIG models are published in full. All calibration parameters are proprietary to The Picken Governance Institute and are not disclosed.

title: Financializing Compute: The Design of AI Service Trade Markets

detail.title: Financializing Compute: The Design of AI Service Trade Markets
detail.abstract: The global AI inference market—reaching approximately $90–100 billion annually and growing at 18% CAGR—operates without organized exchange infrastructure. We document three market failures: resource misallocation (80% of China’s newly built compute capacity sits idle), price opacity (100-fold price dispersion across providers of equivalent quality), and unhedged risk exposure (85% of enterprises miss AI cost forecasts by more than 10%). Following the market design tradition of Roth [2002] and Budish et al. [2015], we propose the AI Service Right (ASR) as a transferable property right on AI compute and the AI Service Unit (ASU) as a quality-adjusted, cross-platform unit of account grounded in hedonic price theory [Rosen, 1974]. The ASU is modality-neutral: billing prices across text, image, video, and speech modalities are unified via eq-token conversion factors (κimg ≈ 2,667 eq-tokens per image; κvid ≈ 2,667 per second of video; κspc ≈ 7 per second of audio), and modality-appropriate benchmark sets (MMLU/HumanEval for language; FID/CLIP Score for image; FVD/CLIPSIM for video; MMBench for multimodal) supply the quality in dex via PCA. We design a hybrid secondary market architecture synthesizing mechanisms from four orthogonal market traditions: foreign exchange markets (cross-platform exchange rates and PPP-analog arbitrage via the ASU); equity markets (Central Limit Order Book, market making, clearing); electricity markets (Compute Locational Marginal Pricing for spatial scarcity signals); and decentralized finance (Automated Market Maker for long-tail liquidity). We establish nine formal propositions: bilateral trading is generically inefficient; Compute Locational Marginal Pricing decomposes nodal prices into system marginal cost, capacity congestion, and bandwidth premia; no-arbitrage equi librium holds with capital constraints (extending Shleifer and Vishny 1997); the ASR market Pareto-improves over bilateral trading; market prices are more in formative under ASR; the hybrid CLOB-AMM architecture weakly dominates either mechanism alone; platform adoption admits multiple equilibria with a coordination trap; financialization may improve or reduce price informativeness depending on speculator-hedger composition; and a hedonic micro-foundation justifies the ASU definition. Calibrated agent-based simulation (500 steps, 30 Monte Carlo runs) provides computational validation: the hybrid architecture reduces price dispersion by 90% relative to bilateral trading, and order-of-magnitude welfare estimates suggest enterprise procurement cost savings of 0.2–20% (net of ASR transaction costs; see Table 7) and potential TFP gains from compute reallocation of up to $29.9 billion annually. We propose a phased implementation roadmap from shadow ledger to full financialization, and we engage critically with the concern that financialization may not reduce intermediation costs [Philippon, 2015].

detail.abstract: Violence against children (VAC) is a pervasive public health concern with profound and lasting consequences for physical, mental, and social well-being. While prior research has linked economic stressors such as unemployment to child maltreatment, less is known about the association between broader measures of economic development and VAC, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. This study examines the association between state-level GDP per capita and crimes against children across Indian states over time, incorporating police per capita as a secondary indicator of institutional capacity. Using longitudinal administrative crime data from, results of a linear regression with panel correction standard errors, indicate a nonlinear relationship between GDP per capita and crimes against children. Additionally, there is a significant association between policing capacity and reported crimes. By distinguishing between economic development and state capacity, this study contributes new longitudinal evidence from a large LMIC context and underscores the need for caution in interpreting official crime data when designing child protection policy.

title: HDC-YOLO: A Hybrid Detection and Classification Models for Automated Brain Abnormality Detection using MR Images

detail.title: HDC-YOLO: A Hybrid Detection and Classification Models for Automated Brain Abnormality Detection using MR Images
detail.abstract: Accurate detection and classification of brain abnormalities are crucial for timely diagnosis and effective treatment planning using medical images. This paper introduces an innovative method, HDC-YOLO employing the You Look Only Once version 9 (YOLOv9), an object detection method combined with a hybrid classification ensemble model that comprises of Residual Network (ResNet), DenseNet, MobileNet, and EfficientNetV2 architectures for precise detection and classification of abnormalities using Magnetic Resonance (MR) images. Skull stripping to remove non-brain tissues, Anisotropic Diffusion (AD) filter denoising, and Contrast Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLAHE) for contrast enhancement are part of the preprocessing techniques that the proposed method encompasses. Additionally, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are used to augment the datasets. Prior to transfer learning, YOLOv9, a Deep Learning (DL)-based object detection method has been applied. In a single pass, it predicts bounding boxes and class probabilities from an image to identify and localize objects, making it efficient for detection tasks. In MR images of brain disorders, YOLOv9 precisely identifies and segments regions of interest. These methods are combined with a hybrid classification ensemble model to improve accuracy, robustness, and generalization across MR images. The effectiveness of the proposed method HDC-YOLO has been examined on two brain MR image datasets using detailed performance assessment parameters. Further, these aforementioned assessment parameters were also used to compare the credibility of the proposed method to other existing state-of-the-art methodologies. The average accuracy of the proposed methodology is 99.07% and 99.21% for dataset 1 and dataset 2, respectively, demonstrating its potential for advanced analysis of brain MR images.

title: Urbanization and Child Health in India: Declining Mortality but Rising Nutritional Risks
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Kanpur and Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Kanpur

detail.title: Urbanization and Child Health in India: Declining Mortality but Rising Nutritional Risks
detail.abstract: Urbanization is widely associated with improvements in child health through enhanced access to healthcare, sanitation, and infrastructure; however, it may also reshape food environments and living conditions, generating health and nutrition risks. This paper examines the association between urbanization and child mortality and nutritional outcomes in India using district-level nighttime light intensity as a proxy for urban expansion, combined with individual-level data from two rounds of nationally representative surveys. Exploiting spatial variation across districts and temporal variation across birth cohorts, we document a divergent pattern: higher urbanization is associated with significant reductions in neonatal, infant, and under-five mortality, but also with a higher prevalence of adverse nutritional outcomes among surviving children. These associations are heterogeneous, with weaker mortality declines among middle-and lower-wealth households. We also find evidence of a double burden of malnutrition-urbanization is positively associated with both stunting and overweight, while wasting and underweight remain concentrated among socioeconomically disadvantaged groups, particularly poorer households, and children of less-educated mothers. Mechanism analysis suggests that improved maternal and child healthcare utilization is an important correlate of mortality decline, whereas dietary transitions and changing food environments are associated with worsening nutritional outcomes, especially among disadvantaged populations. Overall, the findings highlight a central paradox of the urban transition: while urbanization is associated with improved child survival, it is also linked to rising nutritional vulnerability, underscoring the need for integrated policies addressing both service delivery and food environments.

title: GCCA-Net: Global Context and Comprehensive Attention Network for Medical Image Segmentation
affiliations: University of Shanghai for Science and Technology, University of Shanghai for Science and Technology, University of Shanghai for Science and Technology, University of Shanghai for Science and Technology and University of Shanghai for Science and Technology

detail.title: GCCA-Net: Global Context and Comprehensive Attention Network for Medical Image Segmentation
detail.abstract: Convolutional neural networks have demonstrated their effectiveness in medical image segmentation,having achieved cutting-edge performance. Although numerous attempts have been undertaken to enhance encoder-decoder architectures, there are still challenges such as the combination of global and local contexts, fusion of multiscale features and redundancy. In this paper, a novel encoder-decoder architecture named GCCA-Net is proposed which takes a transformer as the backbone to effectively extract the long-range dependencies of input images. A cascaded multi-scale global context module is proposed to extract multiscale context information of encoder features from the current layer and fuse global and local context through a cross self-attention submodule where the fused feature is passed to the decoder layer as well as the shallower layers of the encoder. In addition, an object-wise attention with residual connection module is designed to focus on the object-related semantic information of encoder features. Besides, three attention mechanisms are adopted to alleviate redundant information of features. The proposed method is assessed on two medical image segmentation tasks including six public datasets, and obtains better performance in GlaS and Kvasir with Dice 94.45% and 92.78% as well as mIoU 89.06% and 91.80%. Extensive experiments verify that the proposed method surpasses state-of-the-art segmentation methods.

title: Digital Financial Literacy: A Comprehensive Review of Literature, Empirical Evidence, and Global Developments A Thirumavalavan, Ph D scholar, Lovely Professional University, India
affiliations: Lovely Professional University and Lovely Professional University

detail.title: Digital Financial Literacy: A Comprehensive Review of Literature, Empirical Evidence, and Global Developments A Thirumavalavan, Ph D scholar, Lovely Professional University, India
detail.abstract: Mobile technology is transforming finance via access to mobile money, new FinTech firms and digital payment platforms. In parallel, demand-side capabilities in digital finance termed digital financial literacy (DFL) are increasingly being recognised as important facilitators of financial inclusion, economic empowerment and sustainable development. Drawing from an updated collection of leading empirical and conceptual studies on digital financial literacy, this paper reviews the main findings of 50 papers on digital financial literacy. Our analysis captures evidence on drivers, gender aspects, impact on development outcomes and policy recommendations across countries at different levels of development. We cover studies from India, Indonesia, China, Africa, Vietnam, Pakistan and cross-country comparisons, using various methodologies such as Structural Equation Modeling (SEM), Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA), Quantile Regression, Panel GMM, Difference-in-Differences, Randomized Controlled Trials, Bibliometric Analysis and Natural Language Processing. Digital financial literacy consistently correlates with and causes improved financial outcomes. Digital financial literacy is found to help with financial decision-making, financial inclusion, reducing income inequality, women’s empowerment, and sustainable development. Papers also identify conditions that moderate the power of digital financial literacy. Poverty, institutions, regulation, gender and digital access are found to moderate the impact of digital financial literacy on inclusion and empowerment. Specific findings we highlight include digital financial product use can be more important than digital financial knowledge, gender differences in digital financial literacy are a key mediator of gender differences in financial inclusion, and FinTech contributes to financial inclusion only when combined with sufficient financial literacy. We conclude with policy recommendations including holistic digital financial literacy interventions, incorporating gender into DFL curriculum, enabling regulations and tiered digital access based on poverty.

title: Banking System Resilience in ASEAN: Evidence from Normalized SRISK Measures and Stress Scenarios

detail.title: Banking System Resilience in ASEAN: Evidence from Normalized SRISK Measures and Stress Scenarios
detail.abstract: This paper applies normalized systemic risk metrics to assess the resilience of banking systems in six ASEAN economies under stress scenarios. Building on SRISK, which quantifies potential capital shortfalls during market distress, this study adopted the three ratios developed by Brownlees and Ruan (2018): SRISK-to-Asset Ratio (SAR), SRISK-to-GDP Ratio (SGR) and SRISK-to-Market Capitalization Ratio (SMR). SAR values across ASEAN remain below 4 percent, indicating limited exposures relative to banking assets while SGR values stay below 6 percent of GDP, signaling broadly manageable macro-financial burdens. Both ratios have declined since COVID-19 pandemic, driven primarily by faster growth of assets and GDP relative to SRISK. However, SMR analysis reveals significant cross-country variation in capital market pressures, with some banking systems facing shortfalls that could necessitate substantial equity issuance. The study underscores heterogeneity in systemic vulnerability across ASEAN and highlights implications for country-specific macroprudential calibration systemic surveillance.

detail.abstract:
This paper develops a block-coordinate homotopy method for computing Markov perfect equilibria in multi-region DSGE models with occasionally binding constraints (OBCs). The algorithm decomposes the equilibrium system into region-specific subproblems solved via semismooth Newton continuation. We prove convergence under a state-dependent coupling bound,
establish an O(m^2) theoretical per-iteration flop-count reduction relative to standard policy function iteration and verify uniform grid convergence. On a synthetic 4-region carbon-taxation model the solver handles 98.7% binding constraints, converges at 30× the theoretical coupling bound, and achieves machine-precision accuracy against closed-form LQ solutions. A carbon policy counterfactual demonstrates that exact OBC projection changes quantitative policy conclusions: smooth log-barrier approximations understate the welfare gain from coordinated tax differentiation by 0.46 percentage points comparable to the estimated loss from unilateral leakage (−1.79%).

title: Child Penalties: Evidence from Canadian Data
affiliations: McGill University

detail.title: Child Penalties: Evidence from Canadian Data
detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of children on parents' labor market outcomes in Canada-commonly referred to as child penalties (Kleven et al., 2019b). Using Canadian administrative data, I estimate child penalties in earnings, labor force participation, and selected firm-level attributes. The long-run child penalty in earnings for women is approximately 35%, with considerable variation across provinces. There is a positive correlation between provincial child penalties and childcare costs, suggesting that higher childcare expenses are associated with larger gender gaps in labor outcomes following childbirth. I exploit the 2006 Quebec parental leave reform, which introduced a more generous parental leave policy. While the reform increased men's take-up of parental leave, it had no significant long-run impact on labor market outcomes. These findings show that the introduction of generous parental leave supports men's participation in caregiving and improves the division of household responsibilities (Patnaik, 2019), without imposing long-term labor market penalties on either women or men.

detail.abstract: Anticipatory action (AA)—the use of forecast‑based triggers, pre‑agreed activities, and pre‑arranged financing to act ahead of hazards—has become a central pillar of humanitarian and climate‑risk governance. Existing evidence demonstrates that AA can reduce losses and improve early recovery, yet most frameworks implicitly assume that hazards are discrete events followed by a recovery phase that can consolidate before the next shock. In contexts of recurrent hazards, this assumption does not hold. This paper examines the limits of event‑centred anticipatory action in Madagascar, where tropical cyclones frequently recur within and across seasons, repeatedly interrupting recovery. Drawing on process‑tracing evidence from cyclone‑affected rural livelihoods, the analysis identifies eleven mechanisms (M1–M11) through which recurrence produces cumulative vulnerability across cyclone–recovery–recurrence sequences. These findings are situated within Madagascar’s nascent and fragmented anticipatory‑action ecosystem and examined through the case of Intense Tropical Cyclone Gezani (February 2026), which serves as an operational stress test. The paper shows that while event‑centred anticipatory action can reduce immediate losses, it generates predictable targeting, legitimacy, and continuity failures under recurrent shocks. To address this gap, the paper proposes Sequence‑Sensitive Anticipatory Action (SSAA) as an evolution of anticipatory practice. SSAA preserves AA’s core architecture while reframing success around a durability criterion: whether interventions enable recovery processes to consolidate before recurrence. The findings suggest that in recurrent‑shock contexts, anticipatory action must shift from prioritising timeliness alone toward stabilising recovery trajectories to achieve durable resilience outcomes.

detail.abstract: Although traceability is becoming a crucial component of global trade, its economic benefits are still not equally distributed. This study highlights a "Compliance Chasm" in which data generation expenses are borne by African producers while value is obtained later on by external actors. The paper presents Sovereign Data Logics as a principles guaranteeing that originating economies own and profit from their trade data as a solution to this asymmetry. It suggests a modular, non-coding data governance structure that connects high-stakes global standards with low-tech production realities. The paper uses the Kaduna-Lagos grain corridor as a case study to show how switching from compliance-driven to sovereignty-driven architectures might unleash "Traceability Dividends." The study comes to the conclusion that transforming traceability from an extraction tool into a platform for active data governance and national value retention is vital for the future of trade in the Global South. This research establishes a foundational theoretical basis for applied system architectures, including TerraVerify, designed to bridge the data-trust gap in global extractives. Background: Preterm birth (PTB) is a leading cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Existing clinical risk assessment tools are limited in their ability to provide early and generalizable prediction using routinely collected antenatal data.

Objective: This study aimed to develop and validate an explainable machine learning (ML) model for PTB risk prediction using routine antenatal care (ANC) data from multiple health facilities in Ethiopia.

Methods: A retrospective multicenter dataset comprising 1,356 maternal records from three health facilities was used. A binary risk stratification (BRS) framework was developed using eight state-of-the-art (SOTA) ML models, including tree-based and tabular deep learning (DL) approaches. The best-performing model was further adapted into a one-month-ahead prediction (OMHP) model by excluding variables occurring close to delivery to preserve temporal validity. Model performance was evaluated using discrimination (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC]), calibration (Brier score), and decision curve analysis (DCA). External validation was performed using an independent dataset from a separate health facility. Model interpretability was assessed using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME).

Results: The dataset included 402 PTB cases (29.6%). The TabPFN-based BRS model achieved an AUC of 0.976 (95% CI 0.958 - 0.993) and a Brier score of 0.050. The OMHP model achieved an AUC of 0.959 (95% CI 0.929 - 0.984) and a Brier score of 0.1376. On external validation, the BRS model achieved an AUC of 0.90 (95% CI 0.845 - 0.947), while the OMHP model achieved an AUC of 0.872 (95% CI 0.810 - 0.925). SHAP and LIME analyses identified prior PTB history, hypertensive disorders, and ANC visit frequency as the most influential predictors. Both models demonstrated positive net benefit across a range of clinically relevant threshold probabilities in DCA.

Conclusion: The proposed explainable ML models demonstrated good discrimination and calibration for PTB risk prediction using routine ANC data in a low-resource setting. The results suggest potential utility for early risk stratification; however, prospective validation in diverse populations is required before clinical implementation.

detail.abstract:
Language-model hallucinations are usually judged one statement at a time. We argue that this pointwise view misses a structural mechanism. When an autoregressive model is trained on strings drawn from a formal system, it induces a stochastic inference graph; across bootstrap replicas this graph crystallises into an ensemble of weak formal systems. Some stable structures are genuine theorem-like regions anchored to the trusted axioms. Others are ghost theories: stable, internally coherent components generated by implicit ghost axioms but lacking a robust path back to the seed. 
     The framework uses four ensemble observables: stability, axiom anchoring, logical damage, and bridge risk. Together they decompose the induced theory into an anchored core, true unanchored extensions, false floating ghost theories, and high-damage failures. We prove a soundness-based truth-uniformity result for connected components of the robust graph and explain ghost formation as a consequence of next-token training, which enforces local coherence without enforcing global genealogical closure. This also gives a topological account of paraconsistency: incompatible contents need not collapse the induced theory when they remain quarantined in disconnected components. 
     Empirically, we study MIU and a bounded Robinson-Q-inspired arithmetic with equality and disequality. In MIU, anchoring reaches precision 0.976 against 0.640 for stability filtering at comparable recall. In the arithmetic setting, anchoring reaches precision 1.000 at the headline configuration, removing 33 stable false statements admitted by stability alone. The phenomenon transfers to a small Transformer trained from scratch; its largest false ghost cluster grows from 16 in the trigram setting to 38. Across 250 bootstraps spanning five independent seedbases every floating cluster is truth-uniform without exception, and approximately fifteen per cent of floating-cluster statements appear in floating clusters of every seedbase, identifying them as invariant biases of the model class on this formal system. Axiom-touch experiments further show that true-content touches yield new sound theorems, whereas false-content touches amplify falsity and sometimes break soundness without explicit contradiction. The resulting picture treats systematic hallucination not as isolated error, but as stable local inference structure without trusted genealogy.

detail.abstract: This article explores the critical and worsening state of gender-based violence (GBV) across Pacific Island Countries (PICs), examining the profound tension between alarming reported prevalence rates and the growing, necessary scrutiny of the statistical evidence underpinning those figures. Drawing from recent fieldwork, commissioned reports, and clinical studies conducted in Fiji, Papua New Guinea (PNG), and the North Pacific, it illuminates how outdated national surveys, methodologically constrained clinical convenience samples, and institutionalized judicial bias collectively distort the region's understanding of, and response to, the crisis. The paper gives detailed attention to the medical and psychological emergency of family and sexual violence (FSV) in Papua New Guinea, including the structural barriers that prevent survivors from accessing the five essential medical services they urgently require. It examines cultural mechanisms, including the bride price tradition and economic dependency, that trap women in cycles of violence. Finally, it introduces and evaluates the Pacific Regional Gender Equality Monitoring, Evaluation, Research and Learning (MERL) Plan as the most structurally significant unified regional solution in a generation, positioned to harmonize data collection, reduce reporting duplication, and foster genuine collective accountability across the Blue Pacific.

title: Estimating Public Market Exposure of Private Capital using Bayesian Inference
affiliations: Independant and Burgiss

detail.title: Estimating Public Market Exposure of Private Capital using Bayesian Inference
detail.abstract: Computing private capital's exposure to the public market (beta) is an important but challenging econometric exercise owing to the illiquid nature of the asset class and limited access to timely and high-quality data. Indeed, published estimates of beta to date have failed to reach a consensus. In this paper we use a high-quality dataset of per-fund cash flows and valuations to fit a Bayesian hierarchical model, providing us with precise estimates of beta for buyout and venture capital funds. In addition, given the size of our dataset we are able to estimate how beta changes with the age of a fund, thereby resolving some puzzles regarding previous estimates of beta based on pooled data.

title: Generative AI in Finance and Data Science: A Review and Financial-Mathematics Validity Checklist
affiliations: University of Nottingham

detail.title: Generative AI in Finance and Data Science: A Review and Financial-Mathematics Validity Checklist
detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence and foundation models are increasingly used in finance and data science for synthetic financial data, option-surface generation, market simulation, scenario construction, financial language modeling, and time-series forecasting. A statistically plausible generated output can still be economically invalid if it violates no-arbitrage, martingale consistency, volatilitysurface admissibility, tail-risk preservation, temporal causality, or privacy constraints. This review studies financial-mathematics-constrained generative AI through a PRISMA-informed systematic evidence map rather than an exhaustive quantitative meta-analysis. It makes four contributions. First, it reports a reproducible 129-record evidence map with source-level search counts, inclusion and exclusion criteria, PRISMA 2020 reporting, and auditable supplementary search logs. Second, it distinguishes the review from generic synthetic-data, time-series generative adversarial network, and finance-specific surveys by adding a finance-data-science validity layer: admissibility, no-arbitrage, path geometry, memorization, downstream Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall, temporal leakage, and model-crowding risk. Third, it organizes constraint injection as soft penalties, hard parameterizations, projection operators, adversarial diagnostics, and temporal masks, thereby translating financial mathematics into trainable objectives and validation rules. Fourth, it provides a lightweight validity-checklist script and an open-data case study. On Kenneth R. French daily market-factor data, the case study shows that distributional distances and stylized-fact summaries can rank generators differently from downstream risk diagnostics: a Gaussian moment-matched generator has modest one-dimensional distributional distance but understates one-percent Expected Shortfall by 57.2 percent, while an under-dispersed generator understates it by 75.4 percent. A block boot-1 strap preserves some tail and dependence features but exactly reuses training returns, illustrating a memorization trade-off. The central conclusion is that generative AI becomes credible for financial data science only when financial mathematics governs architecture, data construction, validation, reporting, and deployment controls.

detail.abstract: The Blinker Jinx Decision Model is a conceptual leadership framework explaining how systems transition from intention to disruption through a dynamic escalation process termed the Signal Arc. Integrating insights from safety science, cognitive psychology, organizational theory, and high-reliability research, the model proposes that leadership failure is rarely sudden; rather, it emerges through ignored weak signals, reinforced near misses, and progressively normalized risk behaviors. The framework is organized around four theoretical pillars: Signal Arc Theory, Cognitive Signal Detection, Decision Escalation Dynamics, and Reinforced Risk Normalization. Together, these pillars explain how organizations move from perceived stability (Green) to friction and emergent instability (Yellow) and ultimately toward manifested disruption (Red). Central to the model is the construct of the Jinx Sensation, defined as a pre-analytical anomaly-detection signal in which leaders intuitively perceive divergence between expectations and reality before conscious analysis fully identifies the cause. The model further introduces the Decision Point, where leaders choose whether to reinterpret and adapt or continue momentum unchanged; the Near-Miss Loop, wherein avoided harm reinforces future risk-taking; and the processes of Risk Drift and Normalized Deviance, through which tolerated deviations gradually become institutionalized. The framework contributes to leadership and safety scholarship by linking micro-level cognition to macro-level organizational failure through a unified escalation pathway. The model argues that disruption within complex systems is inevitable, but escalation into catastrophe is decision-dependent. Importantly, successful outcomes achieved under unmanaged risk may not indicate safety, but latent vulnerability concealed by luck.

detail.abstract: Export baskets reflect broader processes of structural change and economic development. While most studies emphasize the emergence of new export specializations, this paper examines an equally important yet neglected pattern—trade exits, defined as sustained declines in revealed comparative advantage. Using a large sample of economies from 2000 to 2019, we show that trade exits are widespread, with more than one-third of trade specializations disappearing during this period. We document substantial heterogeneity across economies and sectors and identify both product- and economy-level drivers of exits. We pay particular attention to the role of product relatedness and to the growing participation of the People’s Republic of China in the global economy—the so-called “China shock”—in shaping exit dynamics, especially in industrial products. Our findings provide new insights into the dynamics of structural transformation in the global economy, with a focus on Asian Development Bank developing economies.

title: Adaptive Edge-Cloud Orchestration for Large Language Models in Mission-Critical Regulated Environments
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Adaptive Edge-Cloud Orchestration for Large Language Models in Mission-Critical Regulated Environments
detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly considered for mission-critical applications in healthcare, financial services, and regulated enterprise decision support. However, centralized cloud inference alone is often insufficient for environments that require low latency, privacy preservation, explainability, and compliance with emerging artificial intelligence governance frameworks. This paper proposes an Adaptive Edge-Cloud LLM Orchestration framework, named AEC-LLMO, for secure and context-aware deployment of LLM services in regulated environments. The framework combines edge AI, cloud inference, federated learning, policy-aware routing, privacy-preserving preprocessing, explainable AI modules, and auditable compliance logging. Rather than treating edge and cloud inference as independent deployment options, AEC-LLMO dynamically assigns each request to local small language models, confidential cloud LLMs, or hybrid retrieval-augmented pipelines based on sensitivity, latency, task complexity, and regulatory constraints. A lightweight simulation using 10,000 synthetic regulated-domain requests indicates that the proposed approach reduces latency relative to cloud-only mean inference while maintaining higher task utility than edge-only deployment and improving compliance traceability. The paper contributes a concise architecture, an orchestration methodology, and an evaluation template for regulated LLM adoption. The findings suggest that adaptive hybrid AI systems can support scalable and privacy-preserving LLM deployment where static routing, purely centralized inference, or isolated edge models are operationally inadequate.

detail.abstract: Can political violence leave measurable developmental scars across generations? This paper provides evidence that Indonesia's 1965-66 anti-communist killings are associated with persistent penalties in child linear growth, plausibly compounded by three decades of subsequent institutional exclusion under the New Order. Exploiting cross-district variation in predetermined PKI electoral support in 1955 interacted with maternal birth-cohort exposure, I estimate an interaction coefficient of-8.604 cm per unit of district PKI vote share on child height and-1.939 SD on height-forage z-score, implying a predicted child height deficit of approximately 2.6 cm and 0.58 SD in HAZ when comparing children in districts at the 90th versus 10th percentile of historical PKI support. Event-study estimates show no systematic differential pre-trends and effects concentrated within the early-life critical window. The estimates are stable across alternative control-cohort definitions, restriction to non-migrant mothers, sibling comparisons using mother fixed effects, an auxiliary district-specific linear-trend control, a continuous dose-response specification, and placebo exposure windows. Maternal adult height accounts for less than two percent of the estimated childheight deficit, suggesting that direct biological transmission alone does not account for the intergenerational effect; the magnitude is more consistent with an acute developmental shock plausibly amplified by prolonged socioeconomic and institutional constraints on the affected maternal generation.

detail.abstract: Competitive single-supplier contracts utilized by the Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) program are an important cost-containment strategy in the U.S. infant formula market, saving over $1 Billion annually. However, the contracts presented a supply chain vulnerability for the over 30 states contracted with a leading brand that issued a recall in 2022. While the federal government encouraged all states to adopt temporary brand and size waivers to increase program flexibility, the timing of adoption differed, creating a unique quasi-experimental setting. We use retail scanner data and a difference-indifferences framework to assess how both contract status and waiver adoption timing affected consumer purchases of infant formula and potential substitutes. Our results show that states contracted with the recalled brand did not experience a significant reduction in sales of powder formula following the recall, a result largely driven by shifts in brand and product size, allowed by waivers. Additionally, while some states not contracted with the recalled brand were criticized for late waiver adoption, we find no impact of waiver timing on powder formula sales. Finally, we find responses differed across types of substitutes: the recall increased sales of fluid formula (appropriate substitute), increased sales of toddler milk products (less preferred substitute), and did not change sales of ingredients for homemade formula (highly discouraged substitute). This evaluation provides essential information on how WIC contract structure, recalls, and policy interventions affect a unique and vulnerable market that continues to face food safety concerns and remains a central policy issue.

detail.abstract: This paper studies whether public debt revenue can finance Pareto-improving redistribution in a two-state general equilibrium model with limited asset-market participation and public debt of multiple maturities. State-dependent term premia make a stationary maturity portfolio a fiscal instrument: it can implement state-contingent primary deficits even though each government bond is not state-contingent. A disaster-state income tax cut in a policy with transfers directed to workers improves the workers' feasible set, and entrepreneurs are not harmed when the induced labor response raises output and dividends enough to offset the redistribution of resources. Numerical exercises show that the policy is disciplined by two complementary forces: fiscal capacity in the revenue matrix and the labor response required to protect entrepreneurs. The results imply that maturity management can support redistribution by shaping the states in which public debt revenue is raised, rather than merely by changing the timing of government finance.

title: Algorithmic Governance and Financial Reporting Behavior: AI Oversight, Structural Pressures, and Income Smoothing

detail.title: Algorithmic Governance and Financial Reporting Behavior: AI Oversight, Structural Pressures, and Income Smoothing
detail.abstract: Income smoothing is typically interpreted as a discretionary managerial strategy used to influence investor perceptions of firm performance. This study develops the Structural Pressure Model of Income Smoothing to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) and algorithmic monitoring systems reshape financial reporting incentives within contemporary governance environments. The model identifies three interrelated pressures-financial leverage pressure, performance expectation pressure, and oversight pressure-and proposes that AI-enabled monitoring fundamentally alters how these pressures operate. Unlike traditional governance mechanisms, algorithmic systems introduce continuous monitoring, predictive risk assessment, and automated anomaly detection, increasing the perceived cost of earnings volatility. Drawing on agency theory, signaling theory, and institutional theory, the framework conceptualizes income smoothing as an adaptive response to AI-mediated oversight environments. The paper contributes to emerging research on digital transformation in accounting by positioning algorithmic monitoring as a distinct governance mechanism and outlining empirical research pathways for examining its effects on financial reporting behavior.

title: The End of the Fabless Illusion: A Thermodynamic Approach to Phase Transitions in Asset-Light Models and the Mark-to-Market Trap
