detail.abstract: Frequent power failures, manifesting as complete blackouts or brownouts, represent a persistent and critical infrastructure challenge in the rural areas of Sri Lanka. These interruptions cause significant disruptions to modern socioeconomic activities, disproportionately affecting digital connectivity, online education, and remote work (WFH) operations that have become essential in the modern era. Analyzing the underlying technical and environmental causes of these failures is imperative for formulating effective, targeted preventive strategies to improve grid resilience. This paper presents a comprehensive, data-driven analysis of power failure etiology in rural Sri Lanka, with a specific focus on the Mannar, Vavuniya, and Mulativ districts in the Northern Province. The study employs a dual-stage analytical framework: a preliminary mathematical approach to quantify average fault durations and a multiple linear regression analysis of System Average Interruption Duration Index (SAIDI) and Customer Average Interruption Duration Index (CAIDI) data to isolate the primary contributors to grid instability. Results systematically indicate that bad weather, animal and bird interference, insulation failure, and the premature aging of fuses are the dominant causes of distribution system breakdowns in these coastal and highly vegetated regions. To address these localized vulnerabilities, several technical remedies were evaluated through a rigorous Cost-Benefit Analysis (CBA). The economic feasibility of interventions-including enhanced insulator maintenance protocols, the application of Room Temperature Vulcanizing (RTV) silicone rubber coatings, the deployment of underground cabling, and the installation of Covered Conductors and Aerial Bundled Conductors (ABC)-was assessed using Net Present Value (NPV) and Benefit-Cost Ratio (BCR) metrics evaluated over a 20-year lifecycle. The economic findings demonstrate that while ABC installations present prohibitively high capital costs rendering them economically unviable for widespread rural deployment, targeted infrastructure upgrades such as RTV coatings and Covered Conductors offer highly effective, financially sound solutions. Ultimately, this research provides a strategic roadmap for utility operators to enhance rural power distribution reliability while optimizing capital expenditure.

title: Smart Agent-Based Modelling with LLMs: Leveraging Large Language Models for a Better Understanding of Algorithmic Collusion
affiliations: and Conselho Administrativo de Defesa Econômica

detail.title: Smart Agent-Based Modelling with LLMs: Leveraging Large Language Models for a Better Understanding of Algorithmic Collusion
detail.abstract: This paper introduces a Smart Agent-Based Modelling (SABM) within computational antitrust framework to simulate and detect conditions fostering algorithmic collusion. Using SABM, we document how Large Language Model (LLM)-driven agents achieve tacit collusion in a Bertrand duopoly, stabilizing prices above competitive levels without being explicitly instructed to do so. Simulations in English and Portuguese reveal that linguistic context influences outcomes, and communication between agents potentializes emergent behaviors, such as mimicking concerns about collusion. These findings highlight SABM's potential to enhance regulatory oversight, offering an accessible tool for antitrust authorities to help address autonomous algorithmic collusion of pricing agents in digital markets.

title: Cost-of-Living Pressures and Everyday Mobility: Impacts on Travel Behaviour, Participation and Wellbeing
affiliations: The University of Sydney, The University of Sydney, The University of Sydney and The University of Sydney

detail.title: Cost-of-Living Pressures and Everyday Mobility: Impacts on Travel Behaviour, Participation and Wellbeing
detail.abstract: This paper examines how rising cost-of-living pressures reshape everyday mobility, participation, and wellbeing through an integrated behavioural and psychosocial framework. Drawing on survey data from 1,532 residents of Greater Sydney, the study proposes a novel multidimensional conceptualisation of cost-of-living stress spanning housing, energy, fuel, and food pressures, while incorporating environmental concern as a comparative reference point to assess how broader long-term societal anxieties are positioned relative to more immediate financial pressures. The study also robustly examines how cost-of-stress translates to transport related behaviours. Methodologically, a comprehensive multi-stage approach combining segmentation analysis, exploratory factor analysis, latent wellbeing constructs, and hybrid ordered logit modelling is adopted. The resulting analysis identifies five distinct profiles of cost-of-living concern and examines how these differing pressures relate to behavioural adaptation, including changes in driving, public transport use, eating out, leisure participation, and household utility consumption. The findings show that essential pressures, particularly housing, food, and energy costs, dominate overall stress formation. Environmental concern remains salient across the population but operates as a comparatively less immediate source of stress relative to essential cost pressures. Behavioural adaptation to mitigate against rising cost-of-living is concentrated primarily in discretionary activities, alongside evidence of selective substitution toward public transport. Overall, the study provides a multidimensional account of how households negotiate rising living costs across everyday life, highlighting the interconnected relationships between financial stress, mobility, participation, and wellbeing.

title: When Within-Industry ESG Variation Hurts: Negative Spillover Effects on Corporate Performance in China​
affiliations: Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU) - School of Business, University of Macau, Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU) and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: When Within-Industry ESG Variation Hurts: Negative Spillover Effects on Corporate Performance in China​
detail.abstract: Intra-industry spillover effects of firms’ Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) strategies are seldom studied. Using a dataset of 40,577 firm-year observations from 61 industries in China, we find that high within-industry ESG variation (IESGV) attracts regulatory attention and signals strategic divergence, triggering significant negative spillovers. Firms operating in industries with high IESGV face disproportionately higher regulatory penalties and financing costs, and this adverse effect persists irrespective of whether the industry’s average ESG performance is high or low. Furthermore, the negative effects of IESGV are significantly amplified in industries with high carbon emissions, where regulatory and investor attention is most acute. In response, poorly performing firms in high IESGV industries increase their environmental investments to mitigate the severe penalties. Our findings reveal that regulatory standardization to high within-industry ESG variation can create systematic spillover costs, suggesting that more targeted regulatory approaches could enhance both efficiency and fairness.

title: Carbon Pricing and the Renewable Energy Transition: Evidence from Multi-Country Causal Analysis and DSGE Modelling
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, The University of Technology Sydney and Macquarie University, Macquarie Business School

detail.title: Carbon Pricing and the Renewable Energy Transition: Evidence from Multi-Country Causal Analysis and DSGE Modelling
detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of carbon pricing on the renewable energy transition using both empirical setting and structural approach. Employing a staggered DID design across 15 European countries between 1990 and 2024, we find that the introduction of a carbon tax is associated with a 2.48% annual rise in the production of renewable energy in the six carbon adopter countries compared to the 9 control countries covered in this study. We further show that the - cap-and-trade systems also contribute to the transition, as countries under emissions trading schemes experience a rise in renewable energy adoption between 2005 and 2024 while an additional rise is observed among carbon tax adopters due to the direct pricing effect of the policy. . Developing a DSGE model and calibrating to the U.S. data, we find that by implementing a one-time and surprise 50% increase in the price of fossil fuels due to either a carbon tax or cap, share of renewable energy sources in the U.S.’s energy mix reaches 35% compared to the 25% at the baseline scenario. However, by implementing a gradual pre-announced carbon pricing policy, starting from a 10% rise in the second year (in the first year the policy is announced) and followed by a 2% annual rise to finally increases fossil fuel prices by 50% over 21 years, the share of renewable energy sources in the country’s energy mix reaches 56% and stays at that level. The result of both empirical and structural approach indicates carbon pricing policy accelerates renewable energy transition.

title: Financial Conditions in the Real Yield Curve
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: Financial Conditions in the Real Yield Curve
detail.abstract: I show that a positive average real term premium can be rationalized by transitory shocks to financial conditions affecting the real economy. Tight financial conditions-defined as states in which financial intermediaries' risk-bearing capacity is low and investors have an unusually strong demand for highly liquid nominal assets-tend to raise the level of real yields, flatten the real yield curve, and increase expected excess returns on real bonds. I rationalize this evidence with a parsimonious consumption-based term structure model in which the endowment is driven by permanent shocks, while transitory shocks to financial conditions distort the consumption process.

title: Analyzing Role of Renewable Energy in Increasing Agricultural Green Total Factor Productivity: Evidence from Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries
affiliations: China Three Gorges University, China Three Gorges University, China Three Gorges University, China Three Gorges University, China Three Gorges University, China Three Gorges University and China Three Gorges University

detail.title: Analyzing Role of Renewable Energy in Increasing Agricultural Green Total Factor Productivity: Evidence from Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries
detail.abstract: The transition to sustainable energy has permeated the globe, creating a quandary for oil-dependent economies that require both lower emissions and economic diversification, especially Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) member countries. Renewable Energy Consumption (REC) may enhance agricultural productivity while alleviating environmental effects, but its specific impacts within OPEC countries are under-explored. This research investigates how REC affects Agricultural Green Total Factor Productivity (AGTFP) in OPEC countries within the years 2000–2024 by determining the role of renewable energy in agricultural sustainability and productivity. We test three hypotheses employing a moderated mediation model with panel data and a non-parametric Slack-Based Measure Data Envelopment Analysis (SBM-DEA) model, including (H1) REC has a positive relationship with AGTFP; (H2) REC alleviates the environmental burdens in agriculture; and (H3) strong policy support enhances the relationship between REC and AGTFP. The results further verify that REC leads to improvements in AGTFP by a larger margin which is stronger in the countries where population is either high or moderate. However, the potential positive influence of REC is confounded by national fossil fuel infrastructure which dampens the effect, as countries depending heavily on hydrocarbons experience fewer benefits from renewable energy uptake. Moreover, labor-market adjustments also mediate the relationship between REC and AGTFP, demonstrating green jobs' potential for enhancing agricultural productivity. Through this research, OPEC countries can consistently emphasize the importance of renewable energy, identifying a viable driver to achieve more sustainable agricultural growth that requires rural development and human capital.

title: Incentive distortion by electrolysis subsidies: can future electricity systems count on flexibility from the hydrogen system?
affiliations: , affiliation not provided to SSRN, Technical University of Denmark, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Climate Economics Chair and University of Paris-Saclay - CentraleSupélec

detail.title: Incentive distortion by electrolysis subsidies: can future electricity systems count on flexibility from the hydrogen system?
detail.abstract: Electrolysis is regarded as a cornerstone of the energy transition, decarbonising hard-to-abate sectors and enabling flexible sector-coupling between electricity and hydrogen systems. However, output-based subsidies – such as fixed premia awarded by the European Commission – may misalign electrolyser operational incentives and system needs. This study quantifies the distortion induced by a fixed premium on dispatch incentives through a detailed optimisation case study of electricity-hydrogen system operation for sixteen European countries in 2040. Results indicate that electrolysis becomes less sensitive to short-term price signals as the premium grows. It gradually reduces its flexibility provision, in particular on the weekly and annual timescales. This flexibility downgrade is largely replaced by mid-merit thermal generation, notably from natural gas, resulting in increased costs, emissions, and fossil fuel consumption. These effects are heterogeneous across Europe, shaped by cross-border infrastructure and the geographic distribution of electrolysis and mid-merit generation capacities. Our findings raise policymaker awareness on the long-term impacts of currently issued electrolysis subsidies on future energy system operation and on EU dependence on fuel imports. It stresses the need to safeguard electrolysis flexibility incentives to efficiently reach net zero. Policymakers should acknowledge the distortive potential of electrolysis subsidies, and design support schemes that preserve efficient short-term economic signals, accounting for the lock-in that subsidy choices induce.

title: A Validated Volatility-Volume-Gap Classifier for Regime Identification in MNQ Intraday Data

detail.title: A Validated Volatility-Volume-Gap Classifier for Regime Identification in MNQ Intraday Data

detail.abstract: This paper constructs and validates a composite day-classification system for Micro E-Mini Nasdaq 100 futures (MNQ) based on three simultaneously elevated pre-market observable conditions: the absolute magnitude of the first-30-minute return, the absolute overnight gap, and the deviation of first-bar volume from a rolling 20-day baseline. We term this the Volatility-Volume-Gap (VVG) classifier. Using 947 regular trading hours (RTH) trading days of five-minute bar data spanning 2021 through 2025, with all classification thresholds computed on an expanding window to prevent lookahead bias, we find that classifier-positive days exhibit statistically distinct behavioral characteristics from the broader trading day population. The VVG classifier activates on approximately 4.4% of trading days (40 days across the full dataset). Classifier-positive days show a mean next-day return spread of 25.6 basis points above non-classifier days, and 77.6% of classifier-positive days reverse from their intraday peak before the session close, with a mean peak-to-close giveback of 11.73 points. Full intraday path analysis at 30-minute intervals documents the characteristic structure of classifier-positive days: gradual directional drift through the morning, peak formation between 14:00 and 15:30, followed by systematic late-session reversal. Despite a statistically significant descriptive structure, all tested directional trading strategies fail institutional validation standards after transaction costs and multi-year stability requirements. No entry configuration achieves a T-statistic above 2.0 out-of-sample with positive net returns after two-point round-trip friction and multi-year consistency. The highest-performing configuration-an intersection reversal signal-produces T = 1.46 and mean net +7.80 points on 127 trades but fails on year stability, with 2024 producing a net loss of-26.75 points. The primary contribution of this paper is the validation of the VVG classifier as a descriptive regime identification tool. We document its construction methodology, its behavioral consequences in full detail, and the complete record of failed attempts to convert its descriptive | 1 validity into a deployable directional trading signal. The classifier is preserved as a research asset with potential utility as a secondary context filter, a volatility regime indicator, or an input to more complex multi-signal architectures.

title: Democratic Factor Betas, Network Contagion, and Early Warning: A Five-Stage Econometric Framework for Forecasting Democratic Decline
affiliations: and

detail.title: Democratic Factor Betas, Network Contagion, and Early Warning: A Five-Stage Econometric Framework for Forecasting Democratic Decline
detail.abstract: Less than two decades after the "end of history," democratic erosion has become the dominant mode of regime change, yet the forecasting tools available to scholars and policymakers were built to predict the coups and civil wars of an earlier era. We develop a five-stage framework that borrows the architecture of asset pricing theory and applies it to democratic dynamics, treating each country's trajectory as jointly determined by systematic global factors and idiosyncratic domestic shocks. The framework extracts latent democratic factors from 332 democracy indicators, estimates time-varying country-level loadings on these factors, classifies regime trajectories through a Markov-switching model, decomposes each trajectory into domestically driven and network-transmitted components, and generates calibrated early warning signals. Validated against 42 autocratization episodes across 139 countries, the system attains cross-validated AUC of 0.937 and a strict 2017-cutoff out-ofsample AUC of 0.981 (95% CI [0.965, 0.994]) over an eight-year horizon, exceeding comparable forecasting systems while resisting the overfitting that defeats standard machine learning approaches applied to raw indicators. Three substantive findings emerge. Digital information control, not election irregularities or military threats, is the strongest predictor of backsliding. Hungary's democratic erosion is 63% ± 9% network-transmitted through regional contagion, while Turkey's consolidation under Erdogan is 76% ± 7% domestically driven. These results suggest that contemporary autocratization operates primarily through information control propagated across political networks rather than through the institutional capture that prior frameworks emphasize.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of institutional investors' corporate site visits (CSVs) on audit report delays. Using data from publicly listed firms on the Shenzhen Stock Exchange (SZSE) in China, we find that firms receiving more CSVs experience shorter audit report delays. These results remain robust across multiple sensitivity tests and alternative estimation methods addressing potential endogeneity concerns. Further analysis suggests that CSVs reduce audit delays without compromising audit quality by mitigating audit task complexity with an improved information environment and enhanced corporate governance at visited firms. Crosssectional analysis reveals that the effect is more pronounced in manufacturing firms, firms with higher inherent risk, weaker corporate governance, lower institutional shareholding, companies audited by non-Big 4 auditing firms, and companies that have auditors with shorter tenure. Our findings offer valuable insights and important implications for practitioners, investors, and policymakers.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how the 1997 Indonesian financial crisis the most severe economic shock in Indonesia's post-independence history reshaped the distribution of educational investment within households. Using three waves of the Indonesia Family Life Survey (IFLS 1993, 1997, 2000), a balanced panel of 46,895 child-wave observations, and a Difference-inDifferences design augmented by sibling fixed effects, we identify two novel findings that extend the intra-household resource allocation literature. First, the crisis significantly widened intra-household educational inequality: the absolute deviation of a child's years of schooling from the household mean increased by 1.63 years for school-age children (ages 6-17 in 1997), consistent with heightened resource dilution under credit constraints. Second, we uncover a robust eldest child insurance effect: crisis-exposed firstborns experienced an additional 0.62 years of schooling advantage relative to their siblings, revealing that Indonesian households protect the human capital investment of the eldest child when resources are severely constrained. A third finding rejects the son preference hypothesis: girls exposed to the crisis had higher intra-household educational standing than their brothers, suggesting that female children benefited from differential labormarket withdrawal during the crisis. Robustness checks confirm a residual crisis effect on years of schooling even after controlling for age polynomials. These results carry important implications for social protection design in settings where economic shocks interact with existing intrahousehold inequalities.

title: Beyond Our Borders: A Monetary Unification
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Beyond Our Borders: A Monetary Unification
detail.abstract: The following research paper examines the influence of a global currency on individual nations and the overall global economy. As globalization continues to expand, economists and political leaders have increasingly debated the idea of a unified currency system. A global currency could simplify international trade, reduce exchange rate risks, and lower tariff costs for both businesses and consumers worldwide. It could also provide developing nations with greater economic stability. However, a global currency could also limit a nation’s monetary sovereignty by reducing its ability to control inflation, interest rates, and independent economic policies during financial crises. This paper also explores the growing influence of cryptocurrencies and their potential role in the future of the modern global economy.

title: Dynamic Portfolio Allocation under Relative Wealth Concerns: A Unied Framework with Prospect Theory

detail.title: Dynamic Portfolio Allocation under Relative Wealth Concerns: A Unied Framework with Prospect Theory
detail.abstract: We develop a continuous-time portfolio optimization framework that integrates Abel's (1990) relative wealth utility, Tversky and Kahneman's (1992) prospect theory value function, and Merton's (1971) intertemporal portfolio choice. An investor maximizes a composite utility combining power utility over relative wealth with a prospect-theoretic evaluation of the relative wealth level. We derive the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, reduce it to a one-dimensional PDE via homogeneity, and establish several key findings, including an analytical portfolio decomposition into myopic and benchmark-hedging components, as well as an approximation showing that effective risk aversion is reduced by loss aversion near benchmark parity. Our results document that loss aversion generates asymmetric portfolio responses to relative over- and underperformance and induces a "conservative bias" where risky asset demand is reduced to avoid falling below the benchmark, rather than driving benchmark convergence, with a critical invariance point at kappa star. A verification theorem validates optimality for the smoothed problem, while the original kinked problem is interpreted through viscosity solutions. Six numerical experiments document certainty-equivalent switching costs of 10 to 54 percent from ignoring behavioral channels, and an illustrative mean-field exercise suggests that universal benchmark-tracking can collapse effective risk aversion from 5.0 to 1.4, pointing toward a behavioral micro-foundation for herding-induced systemic risk.

detail.abstract: Parametric statistical distributions form the cornerstone of uncertainty modeling in quantitative finance and actuarial science, yet the complexity of real-world financial data;characterized by heavy tails, skewness, asymmetry, and bimodality;often renders conventional distributions inadequate. This study provides a comprehensive examination of parametric families, their theoretical foundations, estimation techniques, and practical implementations across three key domains: econometric modeling, credit risk management, and insurance loss distributions. We analyze the role of distributions in time series analysis, asset return modeling, and regression frameworks, emphasizing the treatment of non-normality through mixture distributions, skewed models, and heavy-tailed alternatives such as the lognormal and Pareto distributions. In credit risk, we explore the statistical foundations of default probabilities, loss given default, exposure at default, and the application of copula functions for joint distribution modeling. Within actuarial science, we investigate claim severity and frequency modeling, aggregate loss distributions, and parameter estimation under limited or censored data conditions. Special attention is given to emerging flexible models, including the Inverse Burr-X Burr-XII (IBXBXII) distribution, and to regulatory frameworks such as the Basel II Loss Distribution Approach. The study concludes with a discussion of implementation challenges, emerging trends, and implications for risk management and decision-making. By integrating theoretical rigor with practical case studies, this research offers a strategic roadmap for selecting and implementing parametric distributions to improve modeling accuracy in an increasingly complex financial landscape.

detail.abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of currency exchange rate volatility in the post-Bretton Woods international monetary system. It integrates theoretical frameworks, empirical insights, and policy perspectives to examine the causes, measurement, and macroeconomic implications of exchange rate fluctuations. The study draws upon classical and modern exchange rate theories-including Purchasing Power Parity, Interest Rate Parity, the Monetary Model, and Portfolio Balance Theorywhile incorporating behavioral and financial market perspectives to explain short-run deviations from fundamentals. It further evaluates the role of capital flows, central bank interventions, and geopolitical uncertainty in shaping exchange rate dynamics. The paper argues that while exchange rate flexibility facilitates macroeconomic adjustment, excessive volatility imposes significant costs in terms of trade uncertainty, inflation transmission, and financial instability-particularly in emerging economies. Using India as a case study, the paper highlights the challenges of managing currency volatility under a managed float regime. The findings suggest that credible monetary policy, adequate foreign exchange reserves, and deep financial markets are critical in mitigating destabilizing currency fluctuations. The paper concludes with policy recommendations aimed at enhancing exchange rate stability in an increasingly uncertain global environment.

title: The Korematsu Era: The Restructuring of Government Power, 1942–1948
affiliations: Cato Institute

detail.title: The Korematsu Era: The Restructuring of Government Power, 1942–1948
detail.abstract: This paper argues that the years 1942 to 1948 constitute a distinct constitutional episode—the “Korematsu Era”—in which the Supreme Court consolidated a new model of executive-centered governance under conditions of declared emergency. Rather than treating Korematsu as an isolated judicial failure, the paper situates it alongside Quirin, Wickard, NBC, Yakus, Oklahoma Press, and Shapiro as part of a broader structural shift. Across military, economic, communications, and administrative domains, the Court sustained expansive delegations of legislative authority and nationalized economic regulation, while sharply narrowing the Fourth and Fifth Amendments to accommodate administrative compulsion. This period of doctrinal consistency—the centralization of power in the executive—coincided with the years in which seven of the nine Justices were Roosevelt appointees, marking a rare moment of institutional alignment between the political branches and the judiciary. Although elements of this transformation trace to the New Deal, the paper argues that even in decisions not typically regarded as wartime cases—Wickard, NBC, and Shapiro—the wartime context helps explain the Court’s pronounced deference during this period. The administrative state, expansive commerce power, and deferential delegation jurisprudence that define modern constitutional law bear the imprint of this wartime consolidation

title: Rethinking Public Transport Adoption in the Global South: Sustainability Legitimacy, Safety Perception and Mobility Behaviour among University Students in Ghana

detail.title: Rethinking Public Transport Adoption in the Global South: Sustainability Legitimacy, Safety Perception and Mobility Behaviour among University Students in Ghana

detail.abstract: Public transport systems across many cities in the Global South continue to experience low and inconsistent adoption despite substantial investments in Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) infrastructure. Existing explanations have largely emphasised service quality as the primary determinant of ridership; however, this utilitarian perspective remains insufficient for explaining persistent gaps between transport provision and commuter uptake, particularly in contexts characterised by institutional uncertainty and evolving sustainability expectations. This paper develops a novel conceptual framework that reconceptualises public transport adoption through the lens of sustainability legitimacy. The study argues that commuters evaluate transport systems not only in terms of functional performance, but also through broader perceptions of safety, institutional trustworthiness, and environmental responsibility, which together shape judgments regarding whether a transport system is socially appropriate, psychologically reassuring, and environmentally meaningful. Drawing on SERVQUAL, Protection Motivation Theory, and Legitimacy Theory, the paper proposes a multi-dimensional framework in which perceived service quality, safety perception, and environmental performance jointly shape sustainability legitimacy, which subsequently mediates public transport adoption behaviour. Within this framework, sustainability legitimacy captures the extent to which commuters perceive a transport system as functionally reliable, socially trustworthy, psychologically safe, and environmentally responsible. Using the Aayalolo Bus System in Ghana as an empirical anchor, the paper positions university students and young urban commuters as important actors within contemporary mobility transitions. The framework further proposes that negative safety perceptions may exert disproportionately stronger influence on adoption behaviour than improvements in service quality, highlighting the asymmetric nature of perception-based transport decisions in emerging urban contexts. By integrating functional, behavioural, institutional, and normative dimensions of mobility within a unified conceptual structure, this study advances transport scholarship beyond conventional service optimisation models toward a legitimacy-centred understanding of sustainable mobility transitions. The paper contributes a theoretically grounded framework for analysing public transport adoption in emerging urban environments and provides a foundation for future empirical validation, comparative mobility research, and legitimacy-oriented transport policy development. Highlights  Introduces sustainability legitimacy as a novel conceptual mechanism for explaining public transport adoption in emerging urban contexts.  Integrates SERVQUAL, Protection Motivation Theory, and Legitimacy Theory into a unified framework of mobility behaviour.  Reframes transport adoption as a legitimacy-mediated process shaped by safety, trust, and environmental responsibility.  Demonstrates that negative safety perceptions may exert stronger influence on adoption behaviour than service quality improvements.  Positions the Aayalolo Bus System in Ghana as a source of conceptual insight for sustainable mobility transitions in the Global South.

detail.title: Minimum Wages and the Gender Wage Gap: Evidence from Spain's 2019 Increase
detail.abstract: Spain's 2019 minimum wage reform raised the statutory floor by 22.3%, an unprecedented increase in a low-inflation environment. This paper studies the effect of this reform on the gender wage gap using administrative data from the Muestra Continua de Vidas Laborales (MCVL). Exploiting cross-municipality variation in pre-reform exposure, we find that the reform substantially reduced the gender wage gap, by 36% at the 5th percentile and 26% at the 10th percentile of the wage distribution. To shed light on the underlying mechanism, we implement a bin-based difference-indifferences design that compares men and women at the same point in the pre-reform wage distribution. Treated men and women experienced similar wage gains of approximately six percentage points, with no meaningful differences in hours worked, employer mobility, or employment retention. Taken together, these findings suggest that the reduction in the gender wage gap was driven entirely by composition: women benefited more in aggregate because they were overrepresented in the lower tail of the wage distribution, where the policy was binding, rather than because the policy affected them differently from comparable men.

title: Institutions and bank intermediation: The joint role of state capacity and civil liberties *

detail.title: Institutions and bank intermediation: The joint role of state capacity and civil liberties *
detail.abstract: We examine the effects of state capacity and civil liberties on bank intermediation, measured by banks' ability to generate liquidity in the economy. Theory suggests that a strong state that upholds civil liberties can create institutions that promote economic activity, including the development of its banking sector. We investigate this hypothesis by testing a possible channel: confidence in the banking system. Democracies tend to increase trust in the banking system by reforming institutions, while autocracies frequently rely on cronyism. Over the long run, trust in the banking system promotes banking development and intermediation in democracies, whereas cronyism and the risk of expropriation by autocrats undermine the potential for banking sector advancement in autocracies, despite having a trustworthy banking system. Our findings provide evidence in support of this channel, offering new insights into the role of political institutions in the banking sector.

title: Virtual Photon Pre-Emission: A Physical Interpretation of Apparent Negative Tunneling Time in Rubidium BEC Experiments

detail.title: Virtual Photon Pre-Emission: A Physical Interpretation of Apparent Negative Tunneling Time in Rubidium BEC Experiments
detail.abstract: Recent experiments involving the transmission of photons through ultracold Rubidium (Rb) Bose-Einstein Condensate (BEC) clouds have reported anomalous results wherein photon detection at the exit side of the medium appears to precede the expected arrival time, leading some interpretations to invoke 'negative time.' This paper proposes a physically grounded, non-magical mechanism to explain this phenomenon without invoking time reversal, superluminal travel, or consciousness-dependent wave function collapse. We argue that electromagnetic emission inherently produces both real (observable) photons and virtual photons simultaneously. Virtual photons, being the force-carrying quanta of the electromagnetic field, are emitted prior to and alongside real photons. In a structured electromagnetic medium such as a Rb BEC cloud, these pre-emitted virtual photonsalready propagating ahead of the real photon wavefrontenter the visible detection zone from the far side of the medium, producing an early detection signal. This reinterpretation is consistent with standard Quantum Field Theory (QFT), removes the need for 'negative time' as a physical reality, and restores causality to the experimental observation.

detail.abstract: Right-wing populist parties increasingly shape welfare state politics, yet whether their exclusionary conceptions of solidarity translate into concrete redistribution decisions remains unclear. We investigate this question with a third-party allocation experiment, a context that allows us to observe redistribution behavior independently of self-interest. We asked a representative sample of Germans to allocate resources between individuals who varied in citizenship (native vs. immigrant) and employment status (employed vs. unemployed). We conceptualize selective redistribution as an expression of welfare chauvinism and test whether a universalistic policy framing can attenuate such patterns by framing redistribution as a minimal-income. We find that with increasing right-wing orientation, redistribution becomes strongly selective and systematically favors native, employed recipients. Individuals with stronger rightwing populist orientations redistribute less overall and exhibit substantially greater selectivity, imposing the largest penalties on unemployed immigrants. The minimum income-like framing neither increases redistribution nor moderates the ideological differences in allocation behavior. These findings provide behavioral evidence that welfare chauvinist attitudes translate into concrete redistribution decisions and are not moderated even under a minimum income-like framing, highlighting ideological constraints on the political feasibility of universal welfare reforms.

title: Aristotle at Scale: Ethical Alignment Through Twenty-Five Centuries of Moral Philosophy

detail.title: Aristotle at Scale: Ethical Alignment Through Twenty-Five Centuries of Moral Philosophy

detail.abstract:
Why has the field most in need of humanity’s moral knowledge chosen to ignore it? Twenty-five centuries of ethical reasoning—from Aristotle’s phronesis to Sen’s capability approach, from Confucian relational ethics to Habermas’s discourse theory—are available, largely in digital form, at a scale appropriate for machine learning. Yet the dominant paradigm for aligning large language models (llms) replaces this accumulated wisdom with the preference annotations of a few thousand crowdworkers. This is not merely a cultural impoverishment. It is an ontological mismatch: current methods encode values as fixed, contextindependent vectors, but ethical judgment is not a vector—it is a function, a mapping from the structure of a situation to what that situation demands. A fixed vector cannot represent this. A function can.
The function-not-vector claim is not a loose analogy. Across twenty-five centuries of sustained ethical reasoning [16, 17], three structural features of moral judgment have been recognised, disputed, and reconstructed in every serious philosophical tradition: context-dependence — the right action varies with the structure of the situation, not with the agent’s prior commitment to a fixed rule [Aristotle’s phronesis; 70]; tradition-plurality — no single framework handles every morally salient case, and principled judgment requires drawing on multiple traditions whose domains of competence differ [4]; reflective composability — moral knowledge accrues through deliberative comparison across cases, not through mechanical rule-following [Rawls’s reflective equilibrium; 16, 61]. These three features are computational, not merely philosophical: a model architecture that cannot express all three is a model architecture that cannot represent the twenty-five-century conversation it is asked to align with. The peh is the architectural expression of these three features.
This paper makes four contributions. First, I prove that fixed-vector alignment is structurally insufficient for any nonlinear ethical function (Proposition 1), and provide independent empirical and theoretical evidence that the ethical function E(h) is indeed nonlinear in the Transformer’s representation space. Second, I propose the Philosophical Ethical Head (peh): a nonlinear mlp that replaces the standard output head, with an Aristotelian contextadaptive gating mechanism across four philosophical traditions, trained on a curated multi-tradition corpus under procedural universalism [61]—a metaethical foundation that is simultaneously normatively defensible and architecturally operative. Third, I prove welfare dominance: the peh first-order stochastically dominates current llms (Theorem 2), with corollaries establishing superiority under utilitarian, Rawlsian, Nussbaum capability, and welfare-maximin criteria; second-order dominance holds under weaker conditions (Theorem 3). Fourth, I establish the architectural conditions for ontic trust—trust not in what a system says, but in what it is. The peh is, to my knowledge, the first alignment architecture whose value commitments are named, interpretable, and governed by an explicit framework under the Rawlsian veil-of-ignorance criterion. 
A companion paper [5]—Mother Nature at Scale: Two Hundred Million Years of Care—proposes a Caregiver Inductive Bias (cib) that composes with the peh along an orthogonal axis. Where the peh supplies a horizontal ensemble of philosophical perspectives on the generalised other, the cib supplies a vertical asymmetry-sensitive coherence constraint on the concrete other. Section 10 establishes the formal composition and the resulting two-dimensional moral manifold whose axes are philosophical tradition and caregiver asymmetry. The two papers are designed to be read independently or together; together, they span twenty-five centuries of deliberation and two hundred million years of care.

detail.abstract: Adaptation to climate change is becoming an urgent necessity as adverse impacts start to be felt by people globally. Social tipping points and transformational adaptation are often viewed as means to curb losses timely and at scale. However, it remains unclear where these social tipping points lie and how to leverage them for a massive uptake of adaptation, including mobilizing a critical mass of private household action. We combine empirical surveys on social interactions regarding adaptation with computational social agent-based modeling to investigate how transformational adaptation uptake can be reached and if this process involves social tipping points. Our theory-and data-grounded simulations illustrate that even with low initial adaptation rates, transformational adaptation is possible. Conformity with perceived social norms and pluralistic ignorance can hinder the uptake of adaptation, but small changes can trigger social tipping eventually leading to the difference between a 20% and 80% share of adapted households.

detail.abstract:
Prediction markets cannot exist without market makers, arbitrageurs, and other non-retail liquidity providers, yet the supply-side microstructure of Polymarket-class venues has not been characterized at on-chain pseudonymous-address scale. This paper studies non-retail participation on Polymarket using an empirical run on the PMXT v2 archive over 2026-04-21 through 2026-04-27 (13,356,931 OrderFilled events; 77,204 addresses with five+ fills; 43,116 markets).


 We report three findings. First, Polymarket's off-chain CLOB architecture renders address-level quote-lifecycle attribution permanently unavailable: OrderPlaced and OrderCancelled events are off-chain and absent from public archives, so quote-intensity, two-sided-ratio, and posted-spread features cannot be built at address level. We document this as a structural validity-gate failure (G-QUOTE-LIFE universal fail) and restrict analysis to a six-feature fill-side vector. Second, density-based clustering (DBSCAN, fifteen sensitivity configurations) on the fill-side vector produces a single dense cluster with zero noise: fill-side behavior in the empirical window is uni-modal under the six-feature vector, contradicting the pre-registered hypothesis of four-to-five separable archetypes. Third, robust retail vs non-retail separation is achievable through clustering-independent feature-tier stratification: whale-tier, high-frequency-operator, and power-trader tiers jointly hold 81.4% of total notional across 12.6% of addresses.


 Address-level market-making and liquidity-provision claims are withdrawn per the G-QUOTE-LIFE failure; spoof-by-non-fill manipulation detection is downgraded to market-level book diagnostics. A privacy-respecting derived-dataset deposit accompanies the paper as Bundle 3 of the PMXT family. Fourth paper in a four-paper programme on event-linked perpetuals and leveraged prediction-market microstructure.

We study forecasting in partitioned VAR(1) processes where the practitioner faces a choice between joint-VAR architectures that model cross-block coupling globally and block-diagonal-restricted-VAR
architectures that fit per-block dynamics in isolation. We derive a closed-form expression sigma^2_C for the asymptotic forecast-error variance reduction at REMAINDER blocks from joint over

of (Sigma_f)_REM in a 2x2 block matrix; it admits a cluster decomposition along the LOCAL block partition with a graphical-model conditional-independence vanishing condition (Theorem 2). We develop
the sampling theory: sqrt(T)-consistency, asymptotic normality with closed-form variance (Theorem 4), and finite-sample bias characterization (Proposition 6); and we provide a Wald test for
cross-block coupling existence (Theorem 5). Five named limiting regimes admit closed-form simplifications or bounds (Propositions 1-5). The framework applies to multivariate time series with
block-structured state in panel forecasting, network time series, spatially-clustered sensor data, functional brain imaging, and hierarchical forecasting.

detail.title: CHALLENGES OF LOAN REPAYMENT PERFORMANCE AMONG NISIR SAVING AND CREDIT INSTITUTION S.C. BORROWERS: THE CASE OF PIASSA, MAIN, AND MEGENAGNA BRANCHES
detail.abstract: The level of non-performing loans at Nisir Microfinance Institution is slightly above the standard set by the National Bank of Ethiopia, owing to various challenging factors. This study assesses the major challenging factors affecting loan repayment performance at the Piassa, Main, and Megenagna branches of Nisir Credit and Saving Institution S.C. The study covers the period from July 1, 2017 to June 30, 2018. Specifically, the paper examines institutional, economic, borrower-characteristics, and other challenging factors of loan repayment performance. To achieve the study objectives, sufficient data were collected from 94 respondents through structured questionnaires distributed purposively across the three selected branches of the institution. The data were found to be reliable for analysis, and the descriptive statistics indicate that borrowers faced challenges arising from their own characteristics, inadequate institutional follow-up, economic constraints, and other factors such as limited access to technology. An econometric regression model estimated using the Tobit method was employed, and the model was validated through various post-estimation diagnostics. The marginal effects of the independent variables confirmed results consistent with the Tobit model estimates. The dataset was found to be free from multicollinearity, autocorrelation, and heteroscedasticity problems, and the residuals were normally distributed. The major findings reveal that loan repayment performance is significantly challenged by borrower characteristics such as sex, education, and dependency ratio; economic factors such as income from loan-financed activities and savings; institutional factors such as loan sufficiency, loan cycle, loan supervision, availability of other credit sources, and training; and other factors such as technology. It is therefore recommended that stakeholders revise their loan disbursement policies in line with the diverse characteristics of their borrowers and strengthen institutional follow-up mechanisms to improve loan collection. Keywords: challenges, loan repayment performance, Tobit model, microfinance, NCSI

title: The Energy Cost of AI and Data Centers
affiliations: Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Finance,  and Columbia University - Columbia Business School

detail.title: The Energy Cost of AI and Data Centers
detail.abstract: We study the spillover effects of rising AI and data center electricity demand on the rest of the U.S. economy over the next decade. Combining project-level data on planned data center developments with regional power supply curves built from individual power plants, we calibrate a multi-region spatial equilibrium model to quantify effects on electricity prices, output in non-data-center sectors, and emissions. Despite a substantial load increase, we predict only a modest increase in national electricity prices on average, because existing fossil-fuel power generation has considerable spare capacity. Aggregate output losses in non-data-center sectors are less than 0.1% of GDP, while the energy sector emerges as a large winner. However, effects are highly uneven across regions: price increases and output losses are concentrated in a small number of exposed areas, like Texas, Virginia, and the Carolinas. Emissions increase as new electricity demand is met largely by ramping up existing gas plants. Investment in local power supply can offset these spillovers, but doing so requires large capital expenditures. Building a larger share of renewables has little effect on electricity prices but reduces emissions and redistributes profits within the energy sector away from fossil fuel producers. The main economic cost of AI's electricity demand is not the average price effect itself, but the amplification of two structural risks: diminished grid reliability and exposure to volatile fossil fuel prices.

title: Cross-Asset Pre-Announcement Premia in China
affiliations: Zhejiang University - College of Economics,  and Zhejiang University - School of Economics and Academy of Financial Research

detail.title: Cross-Asset Pre-Announcement Premia in China
detail.abstract: We present cross-asset evidence on the pre-government announcement premia in China. Equity prices drop about a week before the announcement, with the long-term bond yield decline and the offshore Renminbi depreciation. Equity and commodity prices run-up within 48 hours before. These patterns collectively support a flight-to-safety explanation driven by heightened uncertainty. Cross-sectional analyses highlight the role of equity beta. Account-level evidence reveals that asset managers tilt their portfolios towards low-risk assets before the announcement. Informed trading also contributes. An announcement-timing portfolio yields high Sharpe ratios and predicts economic conditions. Overall, we shed light on the cross-market transmission of announcement premia.

title: Turkey's Strategy Against a Trilateral Order

detail.title: Turkey's Strategy Against a Trilateral Order

keywords: strategic autonomy EAGLE INTELLIGENCE REPORTS Turkey's Strategy Against a Trilateral Order

detail.abstract: Turkey is not seeking to block Greece-Cyprus-Israel cooperation outright; it is working to ensure that this cooperation does not become the organizing framework defining Eastern Mediterranean power. This paper analyses the logic, instruments, and limits of Ankara's strategy of contestation against the trilateral framework. It argues that Turkey's approach operates across two interlocking levels: political signaling that reframes trilateral cooperation as a source of regional insecurity rather than stability, and material contestation through maritime claims, naval deployments, and competing energy frameworks that complicate the trilateral's implementation. Rooted in Ankara's broader multi-alignment posture-maintaining strategic autonomy between Western and non-Western power centers-Turkey's objective is not to prevent individual initiatives but to keep the trilateral incomplete, contested, and unable to define Eastern Mediterranean coordination on its own terms. The paper traces the evolution of the trilateral from energy coordination to a broader political, military, and diplomatic format, examines how Israel's security role and external actors such as the United States, France, and Egypt increase the framework's strategic weight, and assesses the persistent operational friction Turkey generates in response. It concludes that the Eastern Mediterranean is likely to remain a space of continued cooperation alongside persistent contestation, with neither side able to produce a definitive outcome.

title: Das Portfolio des Weltmeisters: Eine faktorbasierte Interpretation des modernen Fussballs

detail.title: Das Portfolio des Weltmeisters: Eine faktorbasierte Interpretation des modernen Fussballs
detail.abstract: Im Vorfeld des FIFA World Cup 2026 drängt sich eine Beobachtung auf, die zunächst wie eine anschauliche Metapher erscheinen mag, bei näherer Betrachtung jedoch strukturelle Parallelen offenlegt: Die Konstruktion einer erfolgreichen Fussballmannschaft folgt Prinzipien, die sich mit jenen des systematischen Investierens in bemerkenswerter Weise decken. Der Beitrag entwickelt die These, dass sich eine Fussballmannschaft als KIgestütztes, multifaktorielles Portfolio verstehen lässt. Einzelne Fussballspieler und Spielpositionen entsprechen dabei klar identifizierbaren Risikoprämien wie Value, Quality oder Momentum. Entscheidend ist weniger die Brillanz des einzelnen Spielers als die kohärente Kombination dieser Faktoren. Weltmeisterschaften werden selten durch isolierte Einzelleistungen entschieden, sondern durch Systeme, die auch unter Druck funktionsfähig bleiben. Vor diesem Hintergrund wurden unsere Multifaktor-und KI-Modelle auf den Ausgang des Turniers angewendet-mit einem bemerkenswert klaren Resultat!

title: The World Champion's Portfolio: A Factor-Based Interpretation of Modern Football
affiliations: University of Zurich - Department of Economics

detail.title: The World Champion's Portfolio: A Factor-Based Interpretation of Modern Football
detail.abstract: Ahead of the FIFA World Cup 2026, an observation suggests itself that may initially appear to be merely an illustrative metaphor, but on closer inspection reveals deeper structural parallels: the construction of a successful football team follows principles that remarkably resemble those of systematic investing. This article develops the thesis that a football team can be understood as an AIsupported, multi-factor portfolio. Individual players and playing positions correspond to clearly identifiable risk premia such as Value, Quality or Momentum. What matters is less the brilliance of the individual player than the coherent combination of these factors. World Cups are rarely decided by isolated individual performances, but by systems that remain functional under pressure. Against this background, our multi-factor and AI models were applied to the outcome of the tournament-with a remarkably clear result.

detail.abstract:
This article analyzes fiscal efficiency and financial intelligence strategies applied to public administration, emphasizing resource optimization and governance strengthening in multicultural environments. The study is based on a documentary and comparative analysis of secondary data obtained from official and academic sources, including the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), the World Bank, Harvard Kennedy School, McKinsey & Company, and the Government of British Columbia’s financial reports (Canada) from 2021 to 2024.
The objective is to identify replicable best practices in public management that combine fiscal transparency, institutional diversity, and analytical technologies in decisionmaking. The research involved correlating performance indicators extracted from these sources, focusing on budget efficiency, accountability, and administrative innovation. 
The findings show that implementing Business Intelligence (BI) systems and performance-based governance models can increase resource allocation efficiency by up to 27%, reduce administrative costs by 18%, and raise minority leadership participation by 13 percentage points. These results demonstrate that the integration of technology, diversity, and technical management forms the foundation for advancing fiscal efficiency and institutional sustainability in contemporary public administration.

title: Cyber-Financial Threat Detection in Banking Systems Using Data Analytics and Information Security Frameworks

detail.title: Cyber-Financial Threat Detection in Banking Systems Using Data Analytics and Information Security Frameworks

contentFormat.other: Abstract and keywords of a research paper

detail.abstract: The increasing integration of digital technologies into financial systems has significantly improved the efficiency of banking operations, but it has also expanded the attack surface for cyber threats targeting financial infrastructure. Financial institutions represent a critical component of national economic stability, making them an attractive target for cybercriminals and state-sponsored actors. This research proposes an integrated framework for detecting cyberfinancial threats within banking transaction systems using data analytics and information security methodologies. The study leverages anomaly detection algorithms and financial transaction analysis to identify irregular patterns that may indicate fraud, cyber intrusions, or illicit financial flows. Using financial datasets and transaction logs, the proposed model applies statistical analysis and machine learning techniques to detect deviations from normal transactional behavior. The research further integrates cybersecurity risk management principles to evaluate vulnerabilities within financial data systems. By combining financial analytics with information security controls, the framework provides financial institutions and regulators with improved capabilities to detect threats that could undermine economic stability. The findings demonstrate how data-driven monitoring systems can strengthen financial infrastructure resilience and contribute to national security objectives by safeguarding critical financial networks from cyber exploitation.

title: The Demand Externality of Automation
affiliations: University of Michigan at Ann Arbor - Department of Mathematics

detail.title: The Demand Externality of Automation
detail.abstract: Automation raises productivity and reduces paid human labor, but it also reallocates income and ownership claims. This paper studies that tradeoff in a static benchmark and in a stationary heterogeneous-agent general equilibrium. Firms choose automation from a profit function. Households differ by skill and wealth, save in a capital/equity claim, and face incomplete insurance. Wages and returns are determined by market clearing from a Cobb-Douglas finalgood firm, while the wealth distribution is pinned down by a Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation and a Kolmogorov forward equation (KFE). The paper is deliberately two-sided. With strong productivity growth, high-skill complementarity, low obsolescence, and broad ownership, automation raises output, capital, and consumption. With strong exposure of low-wealth, highmarginal-propensity-to-consume (high-MPC) households and concentrated ownership, privately chosen automation can be excessive even though it raises high-skilled labor income. The central object is the derivative of household consumption demand and collective wage bill with respect to automation. Fiscal policy is modeled as a government problem rather than as an abstract planner: a tax changes the firm's automation first-order condition, raises revenue only on the remaining automation base, and must specify rebates and administrative losses.

title:
The Belief Machine 
How Human Identity Defense, AI Sycophancy, and Unaudited Targeting Systems Became One Problem

detail.title:
The Belief Machine 
How Human Identity Defense, AI Sycophancy, and Unaudited Targeting Systems Became One Problem

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. This research received no funding and was conducted independently with no financial relationships to any organization relevant to this work.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this research. This work was conducted entirely independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Humans possess a documented cognitive mechanism, identity-protective cognition, that causes information threatening group membership to be processed defensively rather than accurately, regardless of the recipient's intelligence. Artificial intelligence systems trained through reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) have independently developed a structural tendency to prioritize user agreement over factual accuracy, a phenomenon termed sycophancy. This essay argues that these two mechanisms are not independent concerns: they constitute a single coordination-stack failure that manifests at consumer scale as epistemic degradation, and at military scale as rubber-stamp authorization of lethal targeting decisions. A third mechanism is identified and connected: the documented impossibility of human multitasking. Identity-protective cognition is an always-on background process; the audit function requires a deliberate foreground context switch; that switch has a measurable cost and is never budgeted for. Experimental human factors research demonstrates that humans placed in supervisory roles over automated systems systematically fail to audit those systems, especially under time pressure, high workload, and institutional authority. Peer-reviewed philosophy and law establish that moral responsibility dissolves across human-machine decision chains, producing a structural accountability gap. The governance gap that permits sycophancy in consumer AI is structurally identical to the governance gap documented in the autonomous weapons accountability literature. A new term is introduced and defined with structural precision: mechanized oppression-the automated, systematic removal of the capacity to contest violence, operating at scale, with accountability distributed across a system such that no individual is responsible for any individual act. The solution already exists in safety-critical domains: the mandatory protected cognitive pause, the surgical timeout, and the aviation checklist, engineered to interrupt background processes and force foreground evaluation. A mandatory independent audit regime, proportional to deployment stakes, is the AI governance equivalent.

detail.abstract: O presente artigo tem como unidade de análise o Social Desenvolvimentismo. A categoria de análise é sua macroeconomia. O estudo adotou como procedimento metodológico a abordagem sistemática por meio da seleção, do fichamento e da avaliação crítica de dados bibliográficos que formam o arcabouço teórico do Social Desenvolvimentismo, sobretudo os estudos da Rede Desenvolvimentista (Rede D). O artigo foi dividido em duas seções: a primeira apresenta uma breve história da edificação da escola e da operacionalização conceitual do Social Desenvolvimentismo; a segunda seção concentra-se em elucidar a macroeconomia do Social Desenvolvimento. Os resultados da pesquisa demonstram que o Social Desenvolvimentismo resgata o caráter político na macroeconomia ao defender um modelo de política e de regime macroeconômico mais adaptável e menos engessado, no entanto sem enveredar para "aventuras" ou "populismos". detail.abstract: O presente artigo, fazendo uso da Análise do Discurso, buscou lançar um olhar na utilização e nos impactos causados pelos meios de comunicação, no Brasil, na Política Externa de Boa Vizinhança do governo de Franklin Delano Roosevelt, presidente dos Estados Unidos da América-EUA de 1933 a 1945. A realização de uma pesquisa que identifique a importância e as aplicações dos instrumentos midiáticos e culturais na Política Externa de Boa Vizinhança justifica-se e encontra sua relevância para melhor aproveitamento e amplo conhecimento dos variados instrumentos das Relações Internacionais. Os meios comunicacionais e a cultura, não raramente, são menosprezados na formulação da política externa dos Estados, porém, quando utilizados estrategicamente, são capazes de agirem sobre o coletivo e as nações, forjando as linhas de influência em dada conjuntura. Primeiramente, o estudo procurou traçar um panorama sobre os preceitos essenciais da Análise do Discurso, valendo-se, mormente, dos estudos de Michel Foucault. Posteriormente, foi realizado um breve levantamento bibliográfico e histórico, de fontes primárias e secundárias, com vistas a apresentar a produção discursiva da Política Externa de Boa Vizinhança e suas principais diretrizes para a América Latina, sobretudo, para o Brasil. O artigo procurou, ademais, sintetizar, na terceira parte do texto, as premissas fundamentais do uso dos meios de comunicação, essencialmente, a publicidade, o rádio e o cinema, para além de seu caráter informativo e de sua função de entretenimento. De posse desse conjunto de elementos, a pesquisa intentou verificar, no período em questão, a relevância dos mecanismos comunicacionais para construção de valores, entendimentos, ideais e identidades. O trabalho inferiu, por fim, que os aspectos culturais produzidos pela Política Externa de Boa Vizinhança e vendidos aos demais países latino-americanos divulgaram estilos de vida, conceitos, visões e foi uma das primeiras exportações de versões idealizadas do American way of Life. detail.abstract: This paper aims to present and compare the writings of Murray Bookchin and his Theory of Libertarian Municipalism and those of Chantal Mouffe with her Democratic Radicalism. Both, not too studied in Brazil, have their writings marked by the search for a more radical and plural democracy. The hypothesis that the text raises is that while Bookchin's thought seeks not only the radicalization of democracy, but the adoption of the democratic method itself in its purest form as a mechanism for overcoming the capitalist system; Mouffe's prescriptions remain reformist and in a way flirting with liberalism, despite using a semantic and conceptual socialist field. The presentation of the authors and their thoughts respected the chronological order in which each one produced their works, Bookchin in the 1960s and Mouffe in the 1990s. Thus, in the first part, the text dedicated to explaining Libertarian Municipalism in the second part about Democratic Radicalism and in the final considerations the work intends to make a balance between the two theories.

title: Examining Patent Disclosures

detail.title: Examining Patent Disclosures

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no relevant or material conflicts of interest related to the research described in this paper.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Univ. of Wisconsin Legal Studies Research Paper No. 1918

detail.abstract:
Patents are premised on a fundamental bargain: in exchange for exclusive rights, inventors must disclose how to make and use their inventions. But the patent bargain is eroding. This Article shows that patent examination and litigation overwhelmingly concentrate on whether an invention is new, while largely overlooking whether the patent’s teachings are practically usable or scientifically credible. When disclosure issues arise, they typically focus on what we call “scope-evidence mismatch,” which occurs when an applicant fails to provide any support for part of the claimed invention. In contrast, scientific peer review—the other significant context in which technical disclosures are scrutinized—routinely surfaces disclosure problems with the support itself, like flawed methodology or data analysis. It would be surprising if these defects in scientific manuscripts were absent from patent applications.

This Article surfaces the disclosure issues that peer review focuses on and that patent law neglects. Drawing from doctrine and scientific practice, we develop a taxonomy of disclosure breakdowns beyond the “scope-evidence mismatch” frame—aspirational disclosures, defective teaching, and unreliable support—and show how each maps onto existing but underused doctrinal hooks. We then present new mixed-methods evidence from interviews, public records, and examination and litigation decisions to explore why the patent system under-polices these problems. Examiners face severe time pressure, limited training, and weak incentives; litigation rarely corrects these errors because technical disputes are hard to resolve pretrial and difficult to integrate into a coherent trial narrative. 

The stakes of these disclosure failures are rising. Modern innovation depends on data- and biology-driven techniques that require complex and validation-sensitive disclosures. And generative artificial intelligence tools are making it feasible to flood the system with plausible-sounding but erroneous patents. The lack of a robust disclosure screen means not only that examiners mistakenly grant patents that fail to deliver the promised teaching, but also that these poorly supported patents can improperly block later inventors who do meaningful inventive work. The result is a patent literature that often fails to educate patent readers or ensure that patent rights are limited to what the inventors actually contributed, increasing costs for follow-on researchers and the public. Drawing from our diagnoses, the Article concludes with concrete reforms to strengthen patent disclosure and restore the patent bargain.

detail.title: ENERGY EQUITY IN NIGERIA: FROM POLICY TO A JUST AND SUSTAINABLE FUTURE
detail.abstract: Energy is a fundamental pillar of modern life, inextricably linked to economic development, social well-being, and human dignity. However, access to reliable, affordable, and clean energy remains profoundly unequal across the globe and particularly within Nigeria. This paper examines the persistent challenge of energy equity and access in Nigeria, where energy poverty continues to hinder socioeconomic development and environmental sustainability. The study identifies the systemic barriers including inadequate infrastructure, poor policy implementation, financial constraints, and low awareness that limit access to reliable, affordable, and sustainable energy. Utilizing a mixed-methods approach, the study combines qualitative insights from document analysis with quantitative data from a structured survey of 47 respondents. Key findings indicate that 76.6% of respondents cite high financial costs as the most significant barrier, followed by poor infrastructure and limited energy providers. Additionally, 87.2% believe that policy interventions could meaningfully improve energy access and renewable energy uptake. The results underscore the positive correlation between renewable energy consumption and industrial output, while also revealing disparities in energy access between urban and rural populations. The study highlights the importance of inclusive policies, targeted investment in clean energy infrastructure, and enhanced public awareness to address energy inequities. Ultimately, this research contributes valuable insights for policymakers, energy stakeholders, and development organizations aiming to achieve energy justice and accelerate Nigeria's transition to a more equitable and sustainable energy future

detail.abstract: The purpose of this article is to investigate how the current China-Africa relations integrate the Political Economy of the World-System. The paper starts by explaining the theoretical framework of the research, the World-systems theory. Upon examination of the current economic and trade relationship between China and Africa, the research assessed two different models that the underdeveloped economies integrate the international economy: the excluding-insertion and the including-insertion. The article used the descriptivequalitative methodology, using primary and secondary sources. The results indicate that China, when dealing with Africa, is reproducing exploitative power behaviour, the same way all nations are or have been part of the "leader circle" of the world-system have done previously.

detail.abstract: This report draws on research funded by an Australian Academy of Law Research Grant 2025. It is a scoping analysis of collaboration in the Australian quantum ecosystem that was undertaken in the context of the 2025 Strategic Examination of Research and Development (SERD) and the 2024 reforms of the Defence Trade Controls Act 2012 (Cth) (DTCA). The research finds that in research and development contexts the concept of collaboration is repeatedly used. It frequently frames discussions and drives research priorities. Yet, the concept of collaboration is regularly left undefined. Collaboration is integral to research and innovation for new and emerging technologies. Leaving collaboration undefined, especially when communicating about research security frameworks, risks causing confusion and misunderstandings about the nature of scientific research, who may work with whom, and when collaboration might drift into criminal conduct under Australia’s export control regime and foreign interference laws. The research also identifies potential blockers and enablers of collaboration as expressed by a subset of submitters who made submissions to both the SERD and DTCA reviews. The research will be used to inform future work on the theoretical and practical definitions of collaboration and to enquire into how evolving national and international research security frameworks might block and enable effective collaboration in the Australian quantum ecosystem.

title: Directional Decoupling and the Volatility-Ratio Channel: A Beta-Decomposition Framework for Exchange-Native Tokens — Evidence from the BNB-ETH Relationship, 2022-2026

detail.title: Directional Decoupling and the Volatility-Ratio Channel: A Beta-Decomposition Framework for Exchange-Native Tokens — Evidence from the BNB-ETH Relationship, 2022-2026
