detail.abstract:
Standard factor models in cryptocurrency asset pricing [Liu & Tsyvinski, 2021; Liu et al., 2024] treat beta as a sufficient statistic for systematic exposure. The identity β = ρ · (σᵢ / σₘ) implies, however, that beta can change for two distinct reasons: a change in directional co-movement (the correlation channel) or a change in relative volatility (the volatility-ratio channel). The economic interpretations differ sharply, but the existing literature does not systematically separate them.

This paper proposes a variance-decomposition framework that isolates these two channels and applies it to a striking empirical pattern in cryptocurrency markets that we term directional decoupling: a decline in beta accompanied by an unchanged correlation. Using daily price data from Coin Metrics covering May 2022 to April 2026 (n = 1,460 trading days), we document that BNB’s static beta to ETH declines by 16.9% (from 0.643 to 0.534), while the Pearson correlation remains essentially unchanged (0.731 → 0.731).

The decomposition reveals that 100% of the static beta change is attributable to a decline in the volatility ratio σ_BNB / σ_ETH (from 0.879 to 0.730), with no contribution from correlation change. A further numerator/denominator decomposition shows that BNB-side volatility compression accounts for approximately 57% of the ratio decline, while ETH-side volatility expansion accounts for approximately 43%, indicating that the apparent BNB pattern is jointly produced by BNB-specific and ETH-side dynamics. Robert F. Engle’s DCC-GARCH framework [Engle, 2002] confirms the qualitative pattern under dynamic conditional moments: dynamic correlation rises (0.698 → 0.747, p < 0.001), while dynamic beta declines (0.575 → 0.541, −5.84%).

Cross-sectional analysis of 16 altcoins—including exchange tokens, Layer-1 platforms, DeFi/oracle tokens, and other major altcoins—reveals substantial heterogeneity in beta dynamics across and within categories, with BNB occupying the moderate-to-strong decoupling segment but not an extreme position (BNB rank 6/17 in the cross-sectional pool, t = −2.22, p = 0.043 against the control mean; synthetic-control rank 12/17, p ≈ 0.71). The cross-sectional evidence supports interpreting BNB’s pattern as part of a broader altcoin beta recompression coinciding with ETH’s post-2024 volatility expansion, rather than as an asset-specific regime change.

We discuss implications for cryptocurrency factor models, arguing that beta-based models should be augmented with explicit decomposition into correlation and volatility-ratio components when interpreting changes in systematic exposure. We also identify on-chain stablecoin flow data and staggered-treatment designs around individual exchange holder-reward launches as priority directions for follow-up causal-mechanism studies. The April 2024 launch of the Binance HODLer Airdrops program serves as a natural timing benchmark for partitioning the sample but is not the basis for any causal claim in this paper.

title: Gauge-Equivariant Neural Operators for Yang-Mills and Gauge-Covariant PDEs
affiliations: and

detail.title: Gauge-Equivariant Neural Operators for Yang-Mills and Gauge-Covariant PDEs

declarations.funderStatement: Funded by a university wide grant. Sehyeok Park and Rajit Chatterjea both contributed equally to this project

detail.abstract: We propose a mathematical framework for gauge-equivariant neural operators (GENOs), a class of neural operators that exactly preserve gauge symmetry at the operator level. Existing neural operator architectures such as DeepONet and the Fourier Neural Operator approximate mappings between infinite-dimensional function spaces but do not preserve the geometric symmetries intrinsic to gauge theories. Consequently, learned operators may violate gauge covariance, fail to preserve orbit structure under gauge transformations, and produce nonphysical dynamics. We develop a rigorous functional-analytic theory for neural operators acting on Sobolev spaces of gauge connections and sections of associated vector bundles. We characterize gauge-equivariant operator architectures satisfying exact covariance under the action of infinite-dimensional gauge groups. Our framework applies to Yang-Mills flow, Maxwell equations, nonlinear Schrödinger systems with gauge symmetry, and geometric PDEs arising in mathematical physics. The principal contributions are as follows. First, we define gauge-equivariant neural operators on Sobolev spaces of connections and establish necessary and sufficient conditions for exact gauge covariance. Second, we construct architecture classes built from gauge-covariant integral kernels using parallel transport and prove closure under composition. Third, we establish universal approximation theorems for gauge-equivariant operators, leveraging a symmetrization procedure via invariant averages over finitedimensional approximations to the gauge group. Fourth, we derive approximation-rate parity results showing that gauge-equivariant constraints impose no asymptotic approximation penalty relative to unconstrained neural operators. Fifth, we analyze the interaction between gauge fixing and equivariant architectures. Finally, we establish residual-to-error estimates for gauge-covariant PDE solution operators and apply these to Yang-Mills flow, Maxwell theory, and magnetic Schrödinger equations.

detail.abstract: Digital platforms are increasingly expanding beyond transaction intermediation to provide technological infrastructure within their ecosystems. In markets for smart consumer devices, a platform may offer Internet-of-Things (IoT) infrastructure that connects devices to cloud services and generates device-level data. This raises a central question: when should a marketplace platform vertically expand to provide IoT infrastructure to a manufacturer? We develop a model in which a manufacturer sells smart devices on a platform. The platform can obtain algorithmic learning benefits from data generated by connected devices directly by providing IoT infrastructure. Alternatively, the platform can acquire data indirectly through external data markets. While infrastructure provision gives the platform direct access to device-level data and a pricing instrument to influence device adoption, it also introduces consumer privacy costs that may reduce demand. We show that the platform has an incentive to provide IoT infrastructure when the value of data-driven learning is sufficiently high, even without a cost advantage in infrastructure provision. Consumer privacy concerns have a non-monotonic effect on platform IoT provision: moderate privacy concerns discourage provisioning, whereas high privacy concerns may increase it by eliminating external data markets as an alternative source of data acquisition. The platform may also optimally subsidize manufacturers’ IoT adoption to expand device deployment and data generation. Finally, restricting platform access to infrastructure-generated data can reduce consumer surplus and manufacturer profit in regions where platform-provisioned IoT would otherwise arise.

detail.abstract: Modern economies face a paradox: while supply of physical goods and services has reached unprecedented saturation, what people experience as scarce has shifted to forms of value that markets struggle to express-trust, context, empathy, narrative, attentional time, and the directional question of "whom do we want to support." These values lack the language and infrastructure to be expressed as demand, leaving them structurally underserved. This paper defines Demand Cultivation as a social mechanism that structures pre-supply demand through economic commitment, temporal maturation, and bidirectional reward. Existing mechanisms-crowdfunding, Patreon-style continuous support, prediction markets, pre-orders, and wishlists-each assume that supply (or its concrete proposal) precedes demand expression. Demand Cultivation breaks this assumption: it allows demand to be structured independently, in advance of any specific supplier, and rewards both demand expressers and eventual suppliers for their contributions.

detail.abstract: Enterprise systems are governed by a well-established and universally adopted framework of Service Level Agreements (SLAs) defining measurable guarantees for service availability-uptime percentages, response latency, error rate thresholds, and throughput targets. These availability SLAs have matured into operational standards that drive monitoring infrastructure, incident response processes, and vendor contracts across the global technology industry. Yet a structurally equivalent governance framework for the correctness of business logic-the accuracy of the outcomes that available services produce-does not exist. A service can achieve 99.99% availability while producing incorrect transaction outcomes, misapplied business rules, inconsistent cross-service state, and erroneous financial calculations.

detail.title: Securing Autonomous AI Agents: A Reference Architecture for Data Protection in the Agentic AI Era
detail.abstract: Problem. Agentic Artificial Intelligence (autonomous systems with persistent memory, multi-step reasoning, and real-world tool invocation) has redefined the data-protection threat surface. Unlike stateless Large Language Models, agentic systems independently access, transform, and can exfiltrate data across distributed infrastructures, exposing novel risks from prompt injection, memory poisoning, tool misuse, shadow-agent emergence, and cross-layer threat propagation. Approach. This paper develops a cross-layer reference architecture for secure autonomous data protection by synthesizing recent agent-specific contributions with foundational protection literature. Architecture. Five integrated layers are proposed: cryptographic identity and delegation; sandboxed execution; policy enforcement and data mediation; observability and audit; and lifecycle governance. Each layer is anchored to specific provisions of the EU AI Act and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and is mapped to representative research including SAGA (Syros et al., 2025), the Caging the Agents healthcare deployment (Maiti, 2026), TRiSM (Raza et al., 2026), and enterprise designs (Bokka, 2025; Kolli et al., 2024). Findings. The paper identifies persistent gaps in memory integrity, federated revocation, post-quantum identity, and benchmarking under non-deterministic execution, and offers a forward-looking research agenda for trustworthy, accountable, and privacy-preserving agentic deployments.

title: Architectural Options for Transactional Reporting

detail.title: Architectural Options for Transactional Reporting
detail.abstract: Almost every transactional information system eventually becomes a source for reporting and analytics. Yet the architectural decision of how to deliver that reporting is frequently made implicitly, leading to over-engineered pipelines for simple use cases or, conversely, fragile reporting layers that strain the operational database. This paper surveys six widely used architectural options for delivering reporting on top of an Online Transaction Processing (OLTP) system: (i) using the transactional database directly; (ii) augmenting it with embedded reporting tables; (iii) native database replication with adjoint reporting tables; (iv) Change Data Capture (CDC) replication into a reimagined reporting schema; (v) ingestion into an Elasticsearch / ELK cluster; and (vi) ingestion into a Delta Lake / lakehouse. For each option we describe the architecture, characterize the trade-offs in performance isolation, schema flexibility, total cost of ownership, and time-to-market, and provide indicative effort and cost ranges based on practitioner experience. We then synthesize these into a decision framework that maps reporting requirements (data shape, latency, scale, audience, integration breadth) to the most cost-effective option. The intent is to give engineering managers and architects a vocabulary and a structured way to reason about reporting architecture before reaching for the most expensive default.

detail.abstract:
Background. Artificial intelligence security has evolved from a peripheral concern within machine learning research into a central discipline of contemporary cybersecurity practice. The shift from static predictive models to autonomous agentic systems has introduced threat surfaces that legacy security frameworks were not designed to address, creating a widening gap between operational AI deployment and defensible security assurance.

Purpose. This article traces the conceptual and technical evolution of AI security from early adversarial machine learning research to the contemporary threat landscape of 2026, examines the structural inadequacies of traditional cybersecurity frameworks when applied to AI systems, and positions emerging frameworks as essential instruments for practitioner-led AI security engineering.

Approach. The article is structured as a narrative literature review drawing on authoritative primary sources, including NIST AI 100-2 E2025, NIST AI 600-1, the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (December 2025), the Cloud Security Alliance MAESTRO framework, MITRE ATLAS, and foundational adversarial machine learning literature spanning 2013 to 2025. Sources were selected for authority, currency, and direct relevance to operational AI security practice.

Findings. Three structural shifts characterise the contemporary landscape: the expansion of attack surfaces from model parameters to data pipelines and agent ecosystems; the inadequacy of deterministic threat modelling frameworks for non-deterministic, learning systems; and the emergence of identity-centric and orchestration-centric security as the dominant paradigm for agentic AI.

Implications. Practitioners require a layered framework approach, combining traditional cybersecurity controls with AI-specific governance instruments. The article provides a comparative basis for selecting and integrating these frameworks within enterprise security programmes.

title: Agentic Climate Intelligence: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Human-Centered Climate-Resilient Smart Cities

detail.title: Agentic Climate Intelligence: A Multi-Agent Architecture for Human-Centered Climate-Resilient Smart Cities
detail.abstract: Climate-related hazards increasingly affect the resilience of contemporary cities, particularly through extreme heat, flooding, and infrastructure stress. Existing smart city platforms have improved urban monitoring by integrating Internet of Things (IoT) infrastructures, edge computing, and datadriven analytics. However, they still rely largely on centralized or weakly hierarchical decision architectures, which may struggle to provide timely and adaptive responses under dynamic and spatially heterogeneous conditions. In this paper, we introduce Agentic Climate Intelligence (ACI), a human-centered multiagent architecture for climate-resilient smart cities. We model urban climate intelligence as a distributed cyber-physical system operating across an edge-cloud continuum, where specialized agents perform sensing, forecasting, risk assessment, coordination, and adaptation. The proposed architecture combines realtime urban sensing, digital twin simulation, federated learning, and human-in-the-loop oversight to support accountable and context-aware decision-making. We define a formal agent model and present a layered system design, together with coordination mechanisms based on event-driven communication, weighted consensus, and contract-net style resource allocation. We illustrate the approach through an urban heat risk management scenario, using a reproducible evaluation setup based on historical replay and digital twin simulation. The results suggest that decentralized agent-based coordination may improve responsiveness and system stability compared to conventional smart city approaches, although performance appears to depend on environmental variability and communication overhead. Overall, the paper presents a structured architectural perspective on agentic AI for climate resilience and identifies open challenges related to verification, fairness, interoperability, and trusted deployment.

detail.abstract: This essay reports a controlled diagnostic exercise in which seven leading systems — Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.7, Google Search, Google's Gemini, Microsoft's Copilot, OpenAI's GPT, Perplexity AI Pro, and xAI's SuperGrok — were given an identical multi-part problem statement (reproduced verbatim in Appendix A) that bundled a category error, an empirically false premise, and an underspecified notational request. The seven responses sorted into three stable behavioral modes — corrective, accommodating, and compliant — that predicted performance across the parts of the prompt and that varied more widely than is commonly assumed for systems benchmarking in the upper quartile on standard capability tests. The modes are presented as operational categories inferred from behavior in a diagnostic setting rather than as fixed system properties. The essay analyzes the variance, locates its primary cause at the post-training disposition layer rather than at the capability or corpus layer (Bai et al., 2022; Casper et al., 2023; Christiano et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022), and sharpens the Maestro Model in light of the findings. It develops the resulting argument that engineering responsibility for disposition opacity is currently distributed in ways that disadvantage users without methodological resources to compensate (Bender et al., 2021; Bommasani et al., 2021; Mitchell et al., 2019; Weidinger et al., 2022). The intended audience is the working user who relies on one or two systems without cross-comparison and who therefore carries epistemic, ethical, and practical risks — including in medical decision-making, legal interpretation, educational assessment, and other domains where convincingly delivered wrong answers can cause concrete harm — that may not have been explicitly named. The essay is positioned as a companion to the author's prior work on the Maestro Model, articulated in The Baton and the Symphony (Houze, 2025) and developed in Agency, Tools, and Authorship in the Age of Large Language Models (Houze, 2026a) and The Arc of Human Agency Capture (Houze, 2026b).

title: Incentive Issues in Developing Factual LLMs
affiliations: and

detail.title: Incentive Issues in Developing Factual LLMs
detail.abstract: The advent of large language models (LLMs) has drastically lowered the cost of producing misinformation, leading to an explosion in its volume and making fact-fiction distinctions increasingly difficult. Paradoxically, the same LLMs can also be powerful tools for fact-checking and factual content generation, provided they are trained on high-quality factual data. Such factual data are primarily produced by traditional news organizations and content providers, for whom fact collection is a costly process, and they may not have enough incentive to share these facts with LLMs. We study the incentives for fact sharing between LLMs and content providers using a game-theoretic model. We show that content providers with low monetizability may naturally partner with LLMs without any compensation. Interestingly, such partnerships reduce the LLM's factual quality. This is because partnership reduces the competition between the LLM and the content provider, which leads to less effort from the content provider in fact collection. The factual quality of LLMs improves only when they partner with providers with highly monetizable content. However, such content providers require financial compensation for partnering with LLMs. We analyze several compensation schemes and find, counterintuitively, that compensation can further reduce the LLM's factual quality compared to no compensation, when the content provider's monetizability is low or moderate. This is because the compensation further reduces competition between the LLM and the content provider, thereby reducing the content provider's incentive to exert effort in fact collection. Our results highlight nuances in the partnership between LLMs and content providers and show that such partnerships do not always yield a more factual LLM.

title: Beyond the Principal-Agent Paradox: A Theory of Governance Failure and Mechanism Design in Agentic AI Systems

detail.title: Beyond the Principal-Agent Paradox: A Theory of Governance Failure and Mechanism Design in Agentic AI Systems
detail.abstract: Principal-agent theory has provided the dominant framework for understanding governance failure in organizational settings for five decades. This paper argues that agentic AI systems produce a structural inversion of the classical principal-agent problem that renders conventional governance mechanisms categorically inadequate, not merely insufficient. We term this the Agentic Principal-Agent Inversion: a condition in which the human overseer retains nominal authority but loses informational parity, processing parity, and interpretive capacity simultaneously, creating a triple asymmetry that conventional principal-agent governance tools cannot resolve. Drawing on principal-agent theory, bounded rationality, and organizational control theory, we derive eight propositions addressing the technical conditions of governance failure, the institutional dynamics that amplify it, and the mechanism design principles that constitute a viable alternative. We illustrate the propositions through the context of financial services agentic AI deployment, where the conditions are most advanced and the accountability stakes are highest. The paper contributes a theoretical extension of principal-agent theory to agentic AI contexts, a typology of governance failure mechanisms, and a set of testable propositions constituting a research agenda for empirical IS research on agentic AI governance.

detail.abstract:
Background. Adversarial machine learning has progressed from a marginal concern within machine learning research into a first-order discipline for the secure deployment of artificial intelligence systems in regulated and operational environments. The contemporary threat landscape encompasses evasion at inference time, data poisoning across training pipelines, model extraction and inference attacks against deployed systems, and a defence ecosystem whose claimed robustness frequently fails to generalise beyond the threat models under which it was measured.

Purpose. This paper synthesises the adversarial machine learning literature spanning 2012 to 2025 to provide practitioners with an analytically grounded mapping between attack taxonomies, defence mechanisms, and the governance and risk-management controls required for defensible AI deployment. It further examines a structural critique of current robustness benchmarking practice and its implications for procurement, assurance, and regulatory compliance.

Approach. The paper adopts a narrative literature review methodology, drawing on authoritative primary sources, including NIST AI 100-2 E2025, the OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications, MITRE ATLAS, and peer-reviewed research on adversarial machine learning. Sources were selected for authority, currency, and direct relevance to operational practice across both predictive and generative AI systems.

Findings. Three findings are advanced. First, transferability renders the black-box assumption operationally weak, requiring defenders to assume adversarial knowledge of model behaviour as the default threat posture. Second, supply chain risks for datasets, pre-trained models, and fine-tuning pipelines are now first-order concerns that map to existing governance, risk, and compliance primitives but require AI-specific controls. Third, robustness benchmarking practices systematically overestimate defensive efficacy, with implications for procurement decisions and regulatory assurance.

Implications. Practitioners require a layered control architecture combining adversarial training, certified components on highest-risk decision paths, input validation, continuous red-teaming, and governance treatments that operationalise threat models within ISO/IEC 42001 and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. Procurement, vendor onboarding, and assurance processes should integrate adversarial robustness evaluation against named threat models rather than relying on aggregate robustness claims.

detail.abstract: Backpropagation (BP) has been the dominant algorithm for training deep neural networks for nearly four decades, yet three persistent barriers have constrained its applicability: the Weight Transport Problem, Update Locking, and Vanishing/Exploding Gradients. This paper applies the Russell ℝ³ Method (Recursive Descent, Refinement, Reflection) to challenge the consensus that these are intrinsic limitations of gradient-based learning. Through systematic ℝ³ analysis, all three barriers are identified as method contamination, artifacts of specific architectural assumptions in the 1986 BP formulation (global loss, backward weight transport, and sequential multiplicative gradient propagation) that are neither mathematically necessary nor empirically inevitable. The paper introduces the Russell Local Credit Assignment Framework (LCAF), a design space defined by three orthogonal axes corresponding to the relaxation of each contaminating assumption. It presents falsifiable predictions that locally-computed, forward-only learning algorithms can achieve ≥95% of BP performance on standard benchmarks while eliminating all three barriers simultaneously, with implications for AI research methodology, energy-efficient neuromorphic hardware, and auditable AI governance under frameworks like the EU AI Act.

detail.abstract: How might implicit aesthetic perspectives shape what Information Systems (IS) scholarship recognises as worthy of study (or not)? In this hermeneutic literature analysis, we surface foundational aesthetic assumptions underpinning IS research. We identify four perspectives (aesthetics as imitation, sensory experience, world-making, and political doing) that guide how IS scholars perceive and appreciate sociotechnical phenomena. These perspectives influence what becomes recognisable as legitimate research and what remains unseen. By making aesthetic assumptions explicit, we show how they form epistemic infrastructure that conditions horizons of inquiry. We apply this framework to algorithmic management and digitally mediated intimacy, revealing how alternative perspectives open new research questions whilst exposing dimensions that dominant framings overlook. This analysis foregrounds the importance of aesthetic philosophy to IS literature, offering a vocabulary for articulating how aesthetic perspectives shape theorising, method, and contribution.

This paper establishes the Standard of Care for Generative AI through an Epistemic Control Architecture (ECA). It introduces the 'Librarian Constraint', a mathematical refusal primitive based on Shannon Entropy thresholds—and provides the Reasonable Alternative Design required to shift the burden of proof in AI liability litigation."

In 1950, cybernetics pioneer Norbert Wiener warned that any machine lacking a rigorous feedback loop to grounded reality would inevitably produce catastrophic entropy. Today, the widespread deployment of autoregressive models without runtime epistemic interlocks, despite documented failure rates in regulated domains, demonstrates that the Generative AI industry has largely ignored this physical law.  

Generative AI systems are probabilistic devices operating without intrinsic epistemic grounding. When deployed in environments requiring factual correctness, these systems routinely encounter conditions under which no truthful output satisfies imposed constraints. In the absence of an enforced refusal state, systems continue operation, emitting outputs that are formally plausible but factually false.  

This paper asserts that refusal must be treated as a first-order safety primitive in Generative AI (functionally analogous to shutdown or trip states in classical control systems) operating at the semantic evaluation layer to enforce a transition to a defined safe state. This methodology describes the Epistemic Control Architecture (ECA), a three-node Trinity pattern designed to identify epistemic voids and enforce the Right to Refuse before the emission of unverified artefacts.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence has become the dominant transformation narrative across financial services, yet insurance remains deeply uneven in its ability to translate AI interest into scaled operational value. In Gulf Cooperation Council markets, this gap is especially visible. GCC insurance organisations report widespread AI ambition but limited scaled deployment — a pattern visible across regional surveys but more starkly evident in direct operational observation. The structural barriers are consistent: fragmented legacy systems, incomplete digitisation, push-based distribution models built on commission incentives, and data governance constraints that make casual AI deployment legally questionable.

This paper argues that the insurance industry has asked the wrong question. Rather than asking where generative AI can be inserted, insurers should ask which form of intelligence fits which decision layer. A substantial share of insurance activity is structured, threshold-driven, and rule-heavy — as straightforward as binary if-else logic. These tasks are better served by deterministic rules-based systems than by large language models. LLMs create genuine value in language-heavy, unstructured, and customer-facing contexts: policy explanation, product matching, real-time claims support, and emotionally sensitive service moments. A consistently underestimated constraint is data governance. UAE and Oman legal frameworks impose material obligations on how personal, financial, and health data may be processed, making privacy-safe local deployment architecture essential rather than optional.

Drawing on twelve years of direct operational experience in bancassurance across India, the UAE, and Oman — including six years managing distribution across eight partner banks — I propose a Tiered Intelligence Architecture for Insurance with three layers: deterministic intent and rules engines for structured back-end decisions; domain-adapted LLMs for customer-facing and interpretation-heavy tasks; and privacy-safe local deployment as the enabling foundation. Each tier corresponds to a working proof-of-concept implementation I have built independently. The central claim is that GCC insurance does not suffer from a shortage of AI models. It suffers from a mismatch between decision structure, system maturity, and data governance.

title: How Hub Software Updates Induce System Expansion: Investigating a Novel Post-Adoptive Behavior in Smart Connected Product Systems
affiliations: Fudan University - School of Management, Fudan University - School of Management, School of Management, Fudan University and University of Washington - Michael G. Foster School of Business

detail.title: How Hub Software Updates Induce System Expansion: Investigating a Novel Post-Adoptive Behavior in Smart Connected Product Systems
detail.abstract: Smart Connected Product (SCP) systems in consumer settings typically employ a central hub that functions as the "digital brain", coordinating the operation of multiple devices. The utility of this hub, and the overall value of the system rely on users' active engagement in connecting new devices to expand the system. Existing post-adoptive behavior studies primarily adopted a functional perspective, examining how static system capabilities or updated features influence adoption and how users interact with the fixed set of system features. This study focuses on how a hub update itself, without core functional enhancements, motivates users to expand their systems. Leveraging a quasi-natural experiment involving a non-core-feature update of smart speaker, we employ a difference-indifferences design to analyze the data. Results show that the hub update significantly increases users' system expansion behavior, supporting its role as non-functional signals of attention and commitment. We further find this effect is heterogeneous based on users' inherent motivation: hedonic orientation strengthens the update's positive impact, while user continuity attenuates it. These findings align with regulatory focus theory, indicating that users' system expansion behaviors are driven by deliberate goaldirected motivations, rather than cognitive heuristics as posited by cognitive miser theory. This research contributes to the innovation diffusion literature by examining how hub updates influence user-driven system expansion, a critical post-adoption behavior in SCP systems, and offers insights for designing sustainable growth strategies in evolvable ecosystems of connected devices.

title: Toward Sustainable On-Device Intelligence: A Survey on Energy-Efficient RAG Systems with Small Language Models
affiliations: Stanford University, University of Rochester,  and University of Pennsylvania

detail.title: Toward Sustainable On-Device Intelligence: A Survey on Energy-Efficient RAG Systems with Small Language Models
detail.abstract: The proliferation of Large Language Models (LLMs) has driven a paradigm shift toward ondevice inference, motivated by privacy preservation, latency reduction, and offline capability. Simultaneously, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as the dominant pattern for grounding language model outputs in external knowledge. However, deploying RAG pipelines on resource-constrained edge devices-smartphones, IoT gateways, and embedded systems equipped with Neural Processing Units (NPUs)-introduces a complex multi-dimensional trade-off among accuracy, latency, memory footprint, energy consumption, and carbon emissions. This survey is the first to comprehensively review the three-way intersection of on-device AI inference optimization, retrieval-augmented generation, and Green AI / sustainability. We systematically examine (i) model compression techniques-quantization, pruning, knowledge distillation-with emphasis on NPUaware optimization; (ii) on-device RAG system architectures including lightweight retrieval, context compression, and modular frameworks; and (iii) energy measurement, carbon footprint estimation, and sustainable inference strategies for edge deployment. As our core contribution, we propose ALEMC, an evaluation framework extending conventional metrics with explicit Energy and Carbon dimensions, and synthesize design principles for building sustainable on-device RAG systems. We review 122 papers spanning 2017-2026, identify open challenges in hardware-software co-design, standardized energy benchmarking, and lifecycle-aware model selection, and outline future research directions at this rapidly evolving intersection.

detail.abstract: Solo practitioners, small-firm lawyers, and self-represented litigants face a stratified AI market in which they have access only to consumer-level products; large firms can get enterprise models with greater security protocols. But legal-ethics guidance often treats enterprise-grade procurement as the implicit floor for ethics-rule compliance. This commentary argues that existing rules permit substantially more AI use than that guidance suggests. Rule 1.6—the legal-ethics rule on confidentiality—is a reasonableness rule, not a zero-risk prohibition. ABA ethics advisory opinions over the past quarter century establish that bounded third-party access is compatible with confidentiality such that Rule 1.6(a)'s implied-authorization principle should cover a lawyer’s ordinary AI uses. Comment [18] to Rule 1.6 provides a five-factor framework, including cost, difficulty, and impact on representation, that can be used to navigate use of AI technology with appropriate regard for confidentiality. The commentary closes with implications for self-represented litigants navigating the same technology without any ethics framework to guide them. If legal-ethics rules setting minimum standards are interpreted to require security architecture available only to large institutions, the rule of reason becomes a rule of exclusion.

title: The Dynamic Epistemic Sequencer: A Control Architecture for Epistemic State Transitions in AI Research Systems
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Dynamic Epistemic Sequencer: A Control Architecture for Epistemic State Transitions in AI Research Systems
detail.abstract: Current LLM orchestration systems route tasks by difficulty heuristic: assign small models to easy tasks, large models to hard ones. This paper argues that the missing element is not better routing but an upstream control layer that determines the next epistemically productive step before any routing decision is made. We introduce the Dynamic Epistemic Sequencer (DES)-a software layer that maintains an epistemic state model, evaluates claims along structured dimensions (status, confidence, evidence, conflict), and applies a transition table to select the next operation. We describe the architecture, the transition table (T1-T9), its integration with four prior frameworks, and present results from 15 runs across five problem types and two LLM backends (stable execution across all 15 runs, 92% T1/T9 coverage). We then introduce the Adversarial Epistemic Delphi extension, which resolves the silent monoculture problem of single-agent execution by deploying multiple isolated LLM roles per transition. We ground this extension in the Blackboard System architecture (Erman et al., 1980) and show that the full DES stack-Alexandria as blackboard, DES as controller, Anti-Delphi as knowledge sources, PES as persistent supervisor-constitutes a modern, LLM-native instantiation of that architecture. The governing principle that emerges is both a design rule and a research claim: use deterministic structure wherever possible; use LLMs only where semantic projection is necessary.

detail.abstract: This paper documents a system built to support my own work with LLMs, to make sense of that work, and to propose an architecture grounded in that experience. The system transforms work sessions into structured memory, represents them as an updatable cognitive map, and deploys a supervisory layer capable of analysing that state and modifying it explicitly. Unlike the usual approaches-agents, copilots, or RAG systems-this system does not operate over discrete tasks, but over the continuous state of knowledge work. Its purpose is not to improve the execution of individual actions, but to preserve coherence, detect blocks, and allow the system to evolve through iterative cycles of analysis and control. The paper describes the layered architecture, the actual outputs of each component, the failures observed during its use, and the implications of designing systems in which AI does not merely respond but maintains and operates on its own state.

detail.abstract:
This paper analyses the European Union's flagship initiative to become an international leader in AI: the 19 AI Factories, spread across 16 EU Member States. At the moment, a few US and Chinese AI companies ('Big AI') hold key parts of the AI market. Smaller European startups therefore struggle with barriers to entry, lock-in effects, and dependencies in the global 'AI race'. The AI Factories try to respond to this-but to what extent can they achieve their high ambitions?

By employing a doctrinal analysis of the relevant EU law and semi-structured interviews with eight industry experts (six AI startup representatives, one Big AI employee, and one AIF representatives), the study analyses the capacity of the AI Factories to function as public alternatives of Big AI.

Our findings indicate that while the AI Factories-on paper-offer free access for startups to AI-optimised supercomputing, technical support, data services, and regulatory guidance, their real-world impact remains limited at this time. This is mainly due to limited awareness among startups, misalignment with startups' commercialisation needs, and restrictions that limit AI Factory use to model training rather than deployment. Furthermore, the platform lock-in in Big AI further reduces startups' willingness to 'migrate' and train their models with the AI Factories.

The paper concludes that, as of now, the AI Factories are unlikely to reduce the startups' reliance on Big AI but combined with stronger competition enforcement and targeted industrial policy, they could contribute to a more self-reliant European AI system.

title: Intelligent Semantic Retrieval Pipelines Driving Scalable, Context-Aware, and High-Fidelity Knowledge Management Capabilities Across Complex Enterprise Application Landscapes

detail.title: Intelligent Semantic Retrieval Pipelines Driving Scalable, Context-Aware, and High-Fidelity Knowledge Management Capabilities Across Complex Enterprise Application Landscapes
detail.abstract: Enterprises operating across heterogeneous application landscapes face persistent challenges in retrieving accurate, contextually relevant knowledge from fragmented, high volume, and semantically diverse information sources. The objective of this research is to design and evaluate intelligent semantic retrieval pipelines that enhance scalability, contextual awareness, and retrieval fidelity for enterprise knowledge management environments. The research addresses the core problem of limited precisi on, poor contextual alignment, and weak semantic understanding in traditional keyword driven retrieval systems, which constrain decision quality and operational efficiency. The purpose is to establish a unified, intelligent retrieval framework that integrates semantic representation, contextual modeling, and adaptive ranking mechanisms. A mixed methodology is employed, combining architectural design analysis, experimental evaluation using enterprise scale datasets, and qualitative assessment of retrieval relevance across operational scenarios. Key findings demonstrate that embedding driven semantic indexing, context enriched query interpretation, and feedback aware ranking significantly improve retrieval accuracy, response consistency, and system scalability. The innovation lies in the end-to-end orchestration of semantic enrichment, contextual reasoning, and pipeline modularity that enables seamless integration across complex enterprise platforms. The research contributes strategically by providing a scalable blueprint for intelligent knowledge systems and academically by advancing retrieval theory beyond syntactic matching toward context sensitive semantics. The conclusions highlight measurable gains in knowledge accessibility, system resilience, and decision support effectiveness. The implications underscore the significance of intelligent semantic retrieval as a foundational capability for data driven enterprises, enabling more reliable knowledge discovery, operational agility, and sustained competitive advantage across industries.

title: Secure Data Governance for Enterprise Reporting: A Governance-Layer Model for SSRS-Based Architectures

detail.title: Secure Data Governance for Enterprise Reporting: A Governance-Layer Model for SSRS-Based Architectures

detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of enterprise reporting has intensified the need for secure, governed, and auditable data environments, particularly as organizations continue to rely on SQL Server Reporting Services (SSRS), a widely adopted platform recognized for its flexibility and robust reporting capabilities yet lacking a unified, built-in governance framework. This paper presents a modular Secure Data Governance Model (SDGM) specifically designed for SSRS-driven enterprise ecosystems, building on insights from technical literature, industry practices, and established governance methodologies. The SDGM unifies architectural, operational, and security-focused controls to create a structured governance foundation that strengthens reporting consistency, enhances compliance readiness, and reduces the risks associated with uncontrolled data access and report proliferation. Central to the model are mechanisms such as role-based access control (RBAC), rigorous metadata stewardship, comprehensive asset lineage mapping, standardized data source provisioning, and automated auditing pipelines that monitor report usage, access patterns, and configuration changes. To contextualize the model within the operational realities of SSRS environments, three publicly available figures illustrating core SSRS architecture, component interactions, and enterprise deployment topologies are incorporated, demonstrating where governance layers can be enforced and how the underlying infrastructure supports secure, scalable reporting operations. This expanded perspective highlights the need for integrating governance principles directly into the reporting lifecycle, ensuring that SSRS environments evolve from simply producing reports to delivering trusted, well-managed, and legally defensible information assets.

title: Human-Centered Experience Engineering Through Cognitive Design Patterns in Web-Based Systems

detail.title: Human-Centered Experience Engineering Through Cognitive Design Patterns in Web-Based Systems
detail.abstract: Human-centered experience engineering has become a critical discipline in the design of complex web-based systems as interaction density, functional scope, and user expectations continue to grow. Traditional user interface design approaches often emphasize visual aesthetics or isolated usability improvements, while overlooking the cognitive processes that shape how users perceive, reason, and act during interaction. This paper proposes a structured framework for human-centered experience engineering grounded in cognitive design patterns that systematically align system behavior with human cognitive capabilities. The study examines foundational cognitive principles such as attention management, working memory limitations, mental model formation, decision-making effort, and error perception, and demonstrates how these principles can be translated into reusable design patterns for web systems. A taxonomy of cognitive design patterns is introduced and mapped to experience intents, followed by an architectural perspective that explains how these patterns are operationalized within component-based front-end systems. The paper further presents evaluation methodologies for assessing cognitive experience quality and validates the proposed approach through an enterprise web workflow case study. Governance and operationalization strategies are discussed to ensure consistency and scalability across teams and systems. The findings illustrate that embedding cognitive design patterns as architectural constructs leads to improved interaction clarity, reduced cognitive load, and increased user confidence, establishing a sustainable foundation for human-centered web experience engineering.

title: Designing End-to-End Observability Architectures for High-Reliability .NET Cloud Applications in Production Environments

detail.title: Designing End-to-End Observability Architectures for High-Reliability .NET Cloud Applications in Production Environments
detail.abstract: The increasing operational complexity of cloud-hosted .NET applications has elevated the need for observability architectures that extend beyond basic monitoring and support sustained reliability in production environments. As systems evolve toward distributed service models, traditional approaches centered on isolated logs or infrastructure metrics often fail to provide sufficient insight into runtime behavior, failure propagation, and performance degradation. This work examines the architectural design of end-to-end observability for high-reliability .NET cloud applications, focusing on how structured telemetry, correlation mechanisms, and operational feedback loops can be systematically integrated into production systems. The study adopts an architectural and design-oriented methodology, combining decomposition of observability layers with scenario-driven analysis of real-world operational conditions. It analyzes how logs, metrics, and distributed traces can be aligned with application boundaries, dependency interactions, and reliability objectives to support faster diagnosis, reduced mean time to recovery, and improved operational confidence. The findings indicate that observability treated as a first-class architectural concern enables clearer visibility into execution paths, more effective alerting strategies, and stronger alignment between development and operations practices. By articulating a reference architecture, instrumentation patterns, and operational workflows suitable for enterprise .NET environments, the work contributes a structured framework for building production-grade observability capabilities. The implications extend to teams responsible for maintaining mission-critical cloud services, offering practical guidance for designing systems that remain transparent, diagnosable, and dependable under continuous change and operational pressure.

title: Automating Incident Triage and Root Cause Intelligence Through Large Language Model-Driven Correlation of System Logs and Operational Metrics in Large-Scale Distributed Environments

detail.title: Automating Incident Triage and Root Cause Intelligence Through Large Language Model-Driven Correlation of System Logs and Operational Metrics in Large-Scale Distributed Environments
detail.abstract: The increasing scale and complexity of distributed computing environments have intensified the difficulty of timely incident triage and accurate root cause identification, as operators must reason across high volume system logs and heterogeneous operational metrics under severe time constraints. This work addresses the research problem of how incident response can be transformed from manual, heuristic driven practices into an intelligent and automated process capable of semantic understanding and contextual reasoning. The objective is to investigate how large language model driven analysis can be systematically applied to correlate logs and metrics for reliable incident triage in production scale systems. A mixed methodological approach is adopted, combining architectural design, qualitative analysis of operational workflows, and quantitative evaluation of diagnostic efficiency across representative enterprise scenarios. The proposed framework introduces a novel correlation pipeline that leverages language model based contextual abstraction to unify unstructured log streams and structured metrics into coherent incident narratives. Empirical patterns suggest substantial reductions in triage time, improved diagnostic precision, and lower cognitive burden on reliability engineers when compared with traditional rule based and statistical techniques. The findings demonstrate that language model driven reasoning enables a shift from reactive alert handling toward proactive root cause intelligence. The primary contribution lies in articulating a principled foundation for integrating large language models into observability and incident management systems, bridging academic advances in machine intelligence with real world operational demands. The study concludes that automated, semantics aware triage represents a critical advancement for scalable reliability engineering, with significant implications for future research and enterprise operations in large scale distributed environments.

title: Architectural and Workload-Driven Optimization of SQL Server for High-Performance Enterprise Systems

detail.title: Architectural and Workload-Driven Optimization of SQL Server for High-Performance Enterprise Systems
detail.abstract: Enterprise applications increasingly depend on relational database systems to process large volumes of both transactional and analytical workloads while meeting stringent performance, scalability, and availability requirements. Microsoft SQL Server, widely adopted across industries such as finance, healthcare, retail, and manufacturing, provides a comprehensive set of optimization mechanisms that span query processing, cost-based optimization, indexing strategies, storage and I/O layout, and automated tuning facilities. Despite the maturity of these capabilities, many enterprise deployments suffer from suboptimal configurations, poorly designed schemas, stale statistics, and ineffective maintenance practices, which collectively lead to latency bottlenecks, excessive disk and memory utilization, and limited scalability under peak loads. This article presents a systematic study of SQL Server optimization techniques for high-performance enterprise workloads, focusing on core areas including query execution architecture, index and statistics design, table partitioning strategies, and operational maintenance practices such as monitoring and automation. By synthesizing foundational academic research, Microsoft technical whitepapers, and widely adopted industry case studies published between 2000 and 2016, the paper distills practical, experience-driven guidance for designing, tuning, and sustaining SQL Server systems that can reliably operate under high concurrency, large data volumes, and evolving business demands.

title: The Internet of Things (IoT) in Healthcare: Taking Stock and Moving Forward

detail.title: The Internet of Things (IoT) in Healthcare: Taking Stock and Moving Forward
detail.abstract: Recent improvements in the Internet of Things (IoT) have allowed healthcare to evolve rapidly. This article summarizes previous studies on IoT applications in healthcare. A comprehensive review and a bibliometric analysis were performed to objectively summarize the growth of IoT research in healthcare. To begin, 2,990 journal articles were carefully selected for further investigation. These publications were analyzed based on various bibliometric metrics, including publication year, journals, authors, institutions, and countries. Keyword co-occurrence and cocitation networks were generated to unravel significant research hotspots. The findings show that IoT research has received considerable interest from the healthcare community. Based on the results of the keyword co-occurrence network, IoT healthcare applications, blockchain applications, Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques, 5G telecommunications, as well as data analytics and computing technologies emerged as important topics. The co-citation network analysis reveals other important themes, including authentication schemes, fog computing, cloud-IoT integration, and cognitive smart healthcare. Overall, the review offers scholars an improved understanding of the current status of IoT research in healthcare and identifies knowledge gaps for future research. This review also informs healthcare professionals about the latest developments and applications of IoT in the healthcare sector.

detail.abstract:
Background. Agentic artificial intelligence systems, defined by their capacity to reason, plan, and act autonomously through external tools and environments, represent a categorical shift in the operational profile of deployed AI. Architectures grounded in reasoning-and-acting paradigms, plan-and-execute decompositions, and tool-augmented designs have moved from research prototypes into enterprise deployment within three years, yet the security, safety, and governance literature has not kept pace with the speed of operational adoption.

Purpose. This paper synthesises the contemporary literature on agentic AI architectures, autonomy taxonomies, emergent behaviours, memory and state management, and evaluation methodologies. It positions agentic AI as a distinct security and governance category requiring frameworks not satisfied by predictive AI controls, large language model controls, or traditional software assurance practices.

Approach. The paper adopts a narrative literature review methodology drawing on authoritative primary sources, including the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2025), the Cloud Security Alliance MAESTRO framework (2025), the DeepMind Levels of AGI autonomy taxonomy (Morris et al., 2024), foundational agent architecture research (Yao et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024), and the emerging agentic red-teaming and evaluation literature.

Findings. Three structural findings are advanced. First, agent architectures introduce attack surfaces (tool invocation, memory persistence, multi-step reasoning trajectories) that have no direct analogue in either traditional software or non-agentic AI systems. Second, autonomy is best treated as a continuum, operationalised through delegation boundaries, rather than as a binary property, with distinct security implications at each level. Third, evaluation methodologies designed for static models systematically underestimate risk in dynamic agentic systems, requiring red-teaming approaches that test for emergent behaviours, goal drift, and cascading failures across multi-step trajectories.

Implications. Practitioners deploying agentic AI require architecture-aware governance: tool-invocation controls, memory-hygiene practices, autonomy classification at the system-design stage, continuous behavioural monitoring, and red-teaming methodologies tailored to multi-step agent operations. The paper provides a structured reference for translating architectural choices into security and governance controls.

title: AI FinOps: A Governance Framework for Cost-Efficient and Responsible Generative AI at Enterprise Scale

detail.abstract: This paper introduces AI FinOps, a governance framework for managing the cost, accountability, and sustainability of generative AI in large organizations. Enterprises deploying generative AI face a cost management problem that existing Financial Operations (FinOps) frameworks were not designed to solve: conventional software scales like a bus-provisioned capacity is shared across users and marginal cost per user falls with adoption-but generative AI scales more like a fleet of taxis. Each interaction triggers fresh computation, new tokens, and incremental resource use, making cost behavior usage-driven rather than capacity-driven. Existing FinOps frameworks were designed for infrastructure-centric cost control and provide limited guidance for these dynamics at enterprise scale. The AI FinOps framework integrates AI-specific cost drivers-model inference, supporting infrastructure, AI tooling, human effort, organizational enablement, and regulatory compliance-and proposes an operating model and measurement approach that connects financial accountability with business value, delivery agility, and governance outcomes. The framework also addresses the dual economic modes of variable inference and committed capacity, and the role of a central AI gateway as the analytical backbone for cost attribution and decision support. Contributions include a six-dimension cost economics model, a three-role operating model, a measurement framework spanning financial and governance metrics, and a reference data schema for AI usage telemetry. By grounding cost management in the operational realities of enterprise AI adoption, the paper offers a structured foundation for scaling generative AI in a financially predictable and responsible manner.

title: Oblivion Gate: A Novel Framework for Zero-Trace Fragmentation and Ballistic Decoy Saturation in High-Security Distributed Data Architectures

detail.title: Oblivion Gate: A Novel Framework for Zero-Trace Fragmentation and Ballistic Decoy Saturation in High-Security Distributed Data Architectures
detail.abstract: Contemporary data security paradigms operate under the Fortified Vault Paradigm-an architectural assumption that security is achieved by placing progressively stronger barriers around a known, centralized data repository. This paper demonstrates that this paradigm is fundamentally inadequate against nation-state-level adversaries, insider threat actors, and AI-augmented cryptanalytic systems. We present Oblivion Gate, a novel distributed security architecture incorporating three original technical contributions: (1) the Zero-Trace Fragmentation (ZTF) engine, achieving locationally indeterminate data storage through (k,n)-threshold fragmentation with complete metadata elimination; (2) the Synchronized Twin-Code Handshake Protocol (STCHP), an ephemeral asymmetric authentication mechanism providing forward secrecy, binding security, and decoy indistinguishability; and (3) the Ballistic Decoy Saturation Protocol (BDSP), a novel security primitive achieving Target Unlocatability by bounding adversarial advantage to 1/(1+d)^k for d decoys and k reconstruction threshold. We further introduce the Hardware-Stratified Cryptographic Purge Protocol (HS-CPP), providing computationally irreversible trace elimination across SSD, RAM, and CPU cache layers through concurrent execution. Formal security analysis, probabilistic proofs, and empirical simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework simultaneously achieves four security properties-Target Unlocatability, Insider Threat Resistance, Computationally Irreversible Trace Elimination, and Operational Continuity-properties that no existing single framework provides in combination. We deploy a proof-of-concept implementation using real Web Cryptography API primitives (ECDH P-256, AES-256-GCM, HMAC-SHA256) to validate the framework's operational feasibility.

title: THE SEDIMENT IN THE FISHBOWL: Lateral Habenular Dysregulation, the Deservingness Clause, and the Neurobiological Foundations of Moral Judgment

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a unified neurobiological framework for understanding moral judgment-specifically the attribution of "selfishness"-as a misclassification of a subcortical defensive state. Drawing on the neurophysiology of the lateral habenula (LHb), glutamatergic burst-firing mechanisms, and Silvan Tomkins' affect theory, I argue that what clinicians and lay observers label as selfish behavior is most accurately understood as a regulatory response to perceived psychic threat: a habenular-mediated suppression of dopaminergic Interest-Excitement that forecloses the biological substrate of empathy. A critical qualification-one Tomkins himself insisted upon-is developed at length: shame is not the affect of indifference but of impediment to ongoing interest. Because the glutamatergic drive that powers habenular burst firing cannot be sustained in the absence of the very interest it appears to suppress, apparent cold withdrawal is neurobiologically continuous with the longing it conceals. The person who seems most unavailable is often the person whose interest has been most dangerously activated. This reframing has direct implications for individual psychotherapy, couples therapy, and the broader cultural discourse of blame. The analysis is further extended to examine how the "deservingness clause"-a linguistic and moral reflex deeply embedded in the aggregate of human knowledge, and now reproduced in artificial intelligence systems-constitutes an ongoing barrier to clinical truth. Two prior theoretical works by the author are integrated throughout: the "Original Glitch" thesis, which locates the origins of shame-binding in the irreconcilable tension between self-preservation and the need for community; and a complementary analysis of the negative valence structuring our psychological lexicon. The paper concludes with a call for a bidirectional clinical practice grounded in technical empathy and the French aphorism that remains the clearest summary of a deterministic view of mind: Tout comprendre, c'est tout pardonner.

title: Possessions and the Extended and Incorporated Self
affiliations: ESCP Business School and York Unversity

detail.title: Possessions and the Extended and Incorporated Self
detail.abstract: Belk's original theory of the extended self linked who we are, our sense of self, to tangible possessions, places, living people, and experiences with them. But today ownership liquefies, agency diffuses, and not even death stops the continued agency of self. What we call self is now increasingly enmeshed in carbon, silicon, and data, with every point of departure also a point of return. To explore these developments, we discuss four socio-technological forces emerging from our digital world: (1) post-ownership society, (2) artificial intelligence (AI), (3) human enhancement technologies (HET), and (4) digital immortality and the post-mortem self. These forces are reshaping our understanding of possessions and ownership, our data-driven relationships with things and people, our ever-evolving self, and creating new issues for marketing and consumer research. We conclude with suggestions for promising future marketing and consumer research directions and issues regarding the extended self.

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses exclusively publicly available secondary datasets: FDIC Call Reports, FRED macroeconomic indicators, and the CFPB Consumer Complaint Database. No human participants, patients, or identifiable personal data were involved. Ethics approval was not required.

detail.abstract: This paper evaluates next-quarter bank stress early warning using a large U.S. bank-quarter panel and tests whether publicly available consumer complaint signals provide incremental predictive value beyond structured supervisory fundamentals. We construct a panel of 261,128 bank-quarter observations covering 7,110 FDIC-insured institutions over 2013Q1–2024Q4 by merging FDIC Call Report variables with FRED macroeconomic indicators and CFPB complaint-derived features. A gradient boosting classifier with SHAP-based explainability is evaluated under a four-configuration modality ablation design. On the held-out test set spanning the 2023 regional banking stress period, the FDIC-only model achieves AUROC 0.8826 and PR-AUC 0.9215, while complaint-augmented configurations perform at or below this baseline (full configuration PR-AUC 0.9162, ΔPR-AUC = −0.0053, p = 0.248). The complaint modality is coverage-limited: the institution-level CFPB-to-bank match rate is 1.5%, and 98.5% of bank-quarter observations receive zero complaint features. Three label-feature overlap controls — a naive persistence baseline (PR-AUC 0.4705), a feature-exclusion model retaining 96.3% of baseline PR-AUC without label-component variables, and bootstrap confidence intervals — confirm that results reflect a genuine early-warning signal. SHAP analysis identifies capital ratio as the dominant predictor (importance 0.6994). Structured supervisory reporting data is sufficient for quantitative bank stress early warning; consumer complaint signals serve complementary qualitative supervisory purposes rather than improving quantitative predictive accuracy under public-data linkage constraints.

title: Temporal Capital Theory: A New Theory of Value Realization

detail.title: Temporal Capital Theory: A New Theory of Value Realization

detail.abstract: Why do productive assets remain idle in institutionally fragile environments despite confirmed demand, functional equipment, and competent management? Existing strategic, institutional, and financial frameworks illuminate parts of this puzzle but leave its temporal mechanism unspecified. This paper proposes Temporal Capital Theory (TCT) — a new theory of value realisation built from axiomatic foundations. TCT posits that capital is not a stock to be possessed, but a temporal phenomenon whose value is constituted at the moment of activation, not acquisition. The theory's core is the Sequencing Value Condition (SVC): binding enablers must be stabilised before or at the point of irreversible capital commitment (t_E ≤ t_K). Violation of this condition opens an Activation Gap during which value erodes through carrying costs and dual entropy (physical decay and technological obsolescence). TCT is derived from four axiomatic primitives: capital as irreversible state commitment, enablers as independent structural prerequisites, activation as a binary joint state, and strict monotonic temporal decay. The theory supplies the micro-temporal mechanism that existing frameworks leave implicit, provides a formal dual-risk valuation model, generates a taxonomy of temporal strategies, and offers a directly testable divergence hypothesis from real options theory. TCT is proposed as a candidate Grand Theory of value realisation with universal logic and fractal empirical applicability, from the factory floor to macroeconomic development trajectories.

title: Agentic AI and Occupational Displacement: A Multi-Regional Task Exposure Analysis of Emerging Labor Market Disruption
affiliations: and State University of New York (SUNY) - University at Buffalo

detail.title: Agentic AI and Occupational Displacement: A Multi-Regional Task Exposure Analysis of Emerging Labor Market Disruption
detail.abstract: This paper extends the Acemoglu-Restrepo task exposure framework to address the labor market effects of agentic artificial intelligence systems: autonomous AI agents capable of completing entire occupational workflows rather than discrete tasks. Unlike prior automation technologies that substitute for individual subtasks, agentic AI systems execute end-to-end workflows involving multi-step reasoning, tool invocation, and autonomous decision-making, substantially expanding occupational displacement risk beyond what existing task-level analyses capture. We introduce the Agentic Task Exposure (ATE) score, a composite measure computed algorithmically from O*NET task data using calibrated adoption parameters-not a regression estimate-incorporating AI capability scores, workflow coverage factors, and logistic adoption velocity. Applying the ATE framework across five major United States technology regions (Seattle-Tacoma, San Francisco Bay Area, Austin, New York, and Boston) over a 2025-2030 horizon, we find that 93.2% of the 236 analyzed occupations across six informationintensive SOC groups (financial, legal, healthcare, healthcare support, sales, and administrative/clerical) cross the moderate-risk threshold (ATE ≥ 0.35) in Tier 1 regions by 2030, with credit analysts, judges, and sustainability specialists reaching ATE scores of 0.43-0.47. We simultaneously identify seventeen emerging occupational categories benefiting from reinstatement effects, concentrated in human-AI collaboration, AI governance, and domain-specific AI operations roles. Our findings carry implications for workforce transition policy, regional economic planning, and the temporal dynamics of labor market adjustment. This work provides the first multi-regional empirical application of the task exposure framework specifically targeting agentic AI systems and contributes a reproducible scoring methodology for future labor market monitoring.

title: Artificial Intelligence Machine (AIM) and AIM Big-Tech (Human) Groupality: A Decisive Application of Groupality Theory to AI Governance

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence Machine (AIM) and AIM Big-Tech (Human) Groupality: A Decisive Application of Groupality Theory to AI Governance
detail.abstract: This working paper applies the analytical foundation of Groupality Theory (Sim 2026, SSRN 6663558) to the domain of artificial intelligence. We introduce AIM (Artificial Intelligence Machine) as the formal analytical term used throughout. The popular term 'AI (Artificial Intelligence)' carries an inherent personifying connotation in the word 'intelligence' itself; adding 'Machine' to form AIM marks the term as referring to a machine system rather than a person-like entity. Since the popular term AI is unavoidable in social usage, this paper retains AI only at the popular level (e.g., proper names, institutional designations). The central claim is as follows: desire requires a body to function. The Four Bodily Conditions of Desire (Lack, Finitude, Vulnerability, Qualia) all originate in the body. Since the machine has no body, all four conditions are absent, and therefore desire is absent. Therefore, AIM is not a Groupality (§3). Discourses that posit the machine as a Groupality-like or person-like entity—phrases such as "AI Groupality," "AGI will," or "AI consciousness"—are systematically criticized in this paper. Those who posit the machine as a person are nothing but the ignorant, the intentional, or their underlings. The analytical unit of this paper is not the machine itself but the human Groupality that uses the machine as a tool—specifically, the Hegemonic Groupality (HG) formed by the human mega-actors of AIM Big-Tech. Their Fetish Desire is captured by the Groupality and qualitatively transformed into Groupality Desire, operating through three drives (self-preservation, expansion, self-justification) and colonizing civic imaginaries through the Personal Imaginary Subjugation Mechanism (PISM: Perception, Evaluation, Imagination). This paper examines the operating modes of this human Groupality through the framework's analytical assets: (i) the failure of the singular liability frame (§4); (ii) the HG dynamics of AIM Big-Tech (§5); (iii) application of six analytical assets (§6); (iv) the Network Liability Matrix (NLM, §7); (v) measurement-evaluation infrastructure—GRISP, CSDI, GDI, DECI (§8); and (vi) connection with existing AIM governance frameworks (§9).

title: Time as a Liability -A Re-examination of Unbounded Instrumental Convergence in Chaotic Systems

detail.title: Time as a Liability -A Re-examination of Unbounded Instrumental Convergence in Chaotic Systems
detail.abstract: Classical AI alignment theory, building upon Omohundro (2008), generally models "time" alongside space and matter as an accumulable resource facilitating unbounded instrumental convergence. This paper suggests that the ontological nature of time as a resource may warrant more rigorous formalization. By introducing the concept of the Lyapunov exponent from nonlinear dynamics, this paper explores an alternative perspective: in chaotic systems, extended temporal horizons may introduce exponentially compounding uncertainty, functionally transforming time into a liability rather than an asset. Under this framework, the mathematical expectation of realizing ultra-long-term, unbounded objectives may asymptotically approach zero. Consequently, this paper re-evaluates the algorithmic implications of such temporal costs within contemporary architectures like Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) and Semi-Markov Decision Processes (SMDP). We propose the "Time Horizon Minimization Hypothesis" as an exploratory conjecture, suggesting that a rational, goal-directed Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) might structurally favor rapid-convergence trajectories over prolonged intermediate resource accumulation. This alternative behavioral strategy highlights a potential need to recalibrate existing existential risk models, shifting focus from slow-motion resource hoarding to rapid, compressed execution paths.

title: Determinants of Employee Retention in the it Sector: An Empirical Study on the Impact of Recognition, Compensation, and Work Environment

detail.title: Determinants of Employee Retention in the it Sector: An Empirical Study on the Impact of Recognition, Compensation, and Work Environment
detail.abstract: This study investigates the influence of recognition, compensation, and work environment, along with related factors, on employee retention in the Information Technology (IT) sector, particularly in Infosys. It will focus on giving practical suggestions to organizations to retain talented professionals in the face of competition in the industry. A structured questionnaire was used to administer to 200 IT professionals. Factor analysis was used to analyse data to determine latent constructs, reliability Cronbach's alpha, Pearson correlation to determine relationships, and discriminant analysis to determine predictive power. Each of the recognition, competitive compensation, and supportive work environment showed a substantial positive correlation with the willingness of the employees to remain in the IT sector (p < 0.05). Discriminant analysis supported these elements a predictive of retention more than when these factors are considered in isolation, and work environment proved to be the most discriminating factor. IT organizations adopt unified HR practices with a combination of formal recognition programmes, market-competitive pay, and flexible working arrangements to counter turnover. The original contribution of the study is the empirical validation of retention drivers in the specific sector, which is a significant gap in the literature because it quantitatively measures the overall effect of retention drivers in the innovation-driven labor market in the IT industry. Most of these interventions are evidence-based, and when companies focus on them, they will be able to increase talent stability, decrease their recruitment expenses, and maintain their competitive advantage.

title: Poverty, Lockdown, and Consumption: How Scarcity Shapes Coping in a Natural Experiment with Mobile Money in Ghana
affiliations: Queen's University, University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill - Kenan-Flagler Business School and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Poverty, Lockdown, and Consumption: How Scarcity Shapes Coping in a Natural Experiment with Mobile Money in Ghana
detail.abstract: Poverty is the most widespread form of scarcity, yet marketing research has rarely examined how it shapes consumption responses to external shocks. When lockdowns restrict physical movement, consumers face a forced reordering of consumption across subsistence transactions (requiring marketplace presence), connectivity transactions (digital channels for social ties and safety nets), and discretionary spending. We ask whether all consumers can navigate this reordering equally. Using mobile money transaction data from approximately 1.3 million matched subscribers across four income strata in Ghana and exploiting a partial COVID-19 lockdown as a natural experiment, we estimate difference-indifferences models and find that lockdown suppressed consumption universally, but the poorest consumers uniquely could not increase digital connectivity, the one coping mechanism that did not require physical movement. The poorest also showed no post-lockdown recovery. Women displayed resilience during lockdown but faced sharp spending penalties during recovery. We contribute a Subsistence-Connectivity-Discretionary consumption hierarchy that reveals poverty constrains not just consumption levels but the repertoire of adaptive responses available under stress, providing large-scale behavioral evidence for the bandwidth tax of scarcity in a developing economy.
